We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLMs' hidden state space, introducing an effective dimension measure d_ρ that achieves 0.93 AUC for distinguishing easy vs. hard MATH500 problems, and showing kinematic features can predict solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens.
AI.motivation: While prior work has focused on the length and content of CoT reasoning chains, their internal geometric structure in the model's hidden state space remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to understand how trajectory geometry relates to task difficulty and solution correctness.
AI.method: Formalizes CoT reasoning chains as discrete curves in ℝ^d; introduces effective dimension d_ρ as a spectral measure of trajectory complexity; computes spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals; validates on MATH500 math reasoning datasets.
AI.result: d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems; kinematic features (mean position, velocity, speed dispersion, etc.) can predict correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens; correctness signatures transfer across problems of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory provides a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality, with potential applications for early-stopping strategies.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: TCA-Captioner is a framework that improves temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning through an iterative refinement strategy (OCC), a curated human interaction dataset, and a diagnostic benchmark (TCA-Bench), achieving state-of-the-art temporally-coherent audiovisual narratives.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based video captioning approaches suffer from modality detachment (failure to bind auditory events to visual entities) and temporal incoherence (inability to capture complex causal dynamics) in audiovisual scenarios.
AI.method: (1) Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) iterative refinement framework for generating high-fidelity grounded training data; (2) TCA-Captioner model optimized on a curated high-density human interaction dataset; (3) TCA-Bench diagnostic benchmark with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol for assessing audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning.
AI.result: TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives, as validated by extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses modality detachment and temporal incoherence in audiovisual video captioning, establishing a new benchmark for temporally-aligned cross-modal narrative generation.

title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
summary: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI coding agents patch compiler missed optimizations in LLVM, finding they often optimize given examples but struggle to generalize to developer-intended scope; historical-knowledge augmentation improves generalization.
AI.motivation: Compiler missed optimizations require significant developer effort to patch. The authors aim to systematically study how well AI agents can patch these issues, identifying the key challenge that patching requires generalization beyond the specific reported case.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues, compare agent-generated patches with developer patches in terms of optimization scope, and introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques (retrieval and distillation from prior LLVM optimization PRs).
AI.result: Coding agents often optimize given examples but many generated patches either cover only part of developer-intended scope, partially overlap, or in some cases generalize beyond the reference patch. Historical-knowledge augmentation improves developer-aligned generalization.
AI.conclusion: Historical-knowledge augmentation techniques leveraging prior LLVM optimization pull requests improve alignment with developer-intended optimization scope and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: LLM agents communicating via text exhibit significant representational homogenization (CAF=0.803), while image communication shows similar coupling (CAF=0.834); group size modulates the effect (K=5 homogenizes, K=3 diversifies), coupling is stateless and prompt-driven, and cross-model replication reveals extreme variation.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether inter-agent communication between LLMs causes outputs to converge (homogenize) or diverge, and to quantify this coupling effect systematically.
AI.method: Introduced BOUNDARY_SYNC protocol measuring Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline). Conducted controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) with text and image modalities, including no-communication ablation, prompt-perturbation controls, group size variation (K=3 vs K=5), cross-model replication, and statelessness testing.
AI.result: (1) Text communication: CAF=0.803 (d=1.30, p<0.001) — significant homogenization; (2) Image communication: CAF=0.834 — comparable homogenization; (3) Group size: K=5 homogenizes, K=3 yields CAF>1.0 (diversification); (4) Cross-model: CAF ranged 0.034–0.803 (extreme variation); (5) Coupling is stateless and prompt-driven.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with implications for multi-agent system design.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: A novel Nested-UNet architecture with inner/outer attention units, squeeze-and-excitation modules, and edge-aware loss that improves multi-scale segmentation and generalization on medical image benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing segmentation methods struggle to capture multi-scale information and perform effective upsampling across different datasets, leading to suboptimal generalization in medical image analysis.
AI.method: Proposes a Nested-UNet architecture with (1) inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, (2) channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, and (3) an edge-aware loss function that prioritizes boundary regions.
AI.result: Tested on three publicly available benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior generalization performance compared to existing Nested-UNet methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided, edge-aware Nested-UNet effectively addresses multi-scale contextual capture and upsampling limitations, achieving state-of-the-art generalization for medical image segmentation.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reformalization (translation between proof assistants) through three implementations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda, identifying key design choices for practical reformalization.
AI.motivation: To understand and improve the process of translating formal proofs between different proof assistants (reformalization), as opposed to autoformalization from natural language.
AI.method: Conducting three concrete reformalization case studies of the Jordan Curve Theorem across different proof assistant pairs and analyzing the pipelines to identify design choices that matter for practical reformalization.
AI.result: Three successful reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem were completed: Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda, with analysis of pipeline design choices that impact reformalization effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies practical design choices for reformalization pipelines, contributing to the broader goal of interoperability between proof assistants.

title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Dataset and evaluation artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21134406
summary: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether giving agentic coding assistants more capabilities (testing tools, design prompts, higher reasoning effort) actually improves software quality. Using 90 independent agent runs building the same application, it finds that capability tier dominates performance, container deployment is the most common failure, testing tools add cost without benefit, higher reasoning effort significantly improves first-try success, and design prompts improve visual quality but not functionality. The key lesson: most failures stem from weak reasoning, not visible flaws that checking tools can catch.
AI.motivation: The assumption that giving agentic coding assistants more capabilities (browser-based testing tools, design-oriented system prompts) leads to better software is widespread but untested. This study directly tests that assumption.
AI.method: 90 independent agent runs built the same real-time retrospective board from one detailed specification. Each run was scored on a 14-criterion functional rubric (42-point max) and a visual quality review. Runs varied across model generations, agent harnesses, reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and design-oriented prompts.
AI.result: Capability tier dominated: frontier models near ceiling, local model at 24-37 points. Container deployment failed first try in 44% of runs. Testing tool raised cost 42-68% without improving functional score or reliability. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh increased first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89% and cut corrective prompts ~5x with 9-29% more cost. Design prompt raised visual quality (4.5 vs 3.0/5) without lifting function.
AI.conclusion: Match the fix to the failure: most first-run failures come from weak reasoning (preventable by stronger model or more effort), not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source automated pipeline that converts circuit schematic images into machine-readable netlists with 96.67% accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art by 2.72x, by integrating deep learning, OCR, and VLMs for component detection, connectivity inference, and crossing-wire disambiguation across both IC and PCB-level schematics.
AI.motivation: Analog and mixed-signal circuit design AI applications are limited by the lack of machine-readable representations (netlists) of existing design knowledge, which is largely stored as schematic images in manuscripts, textbooks, and websites. Current conversion methods lack generalization across IC and PCB domains, struggle with component recognition, connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish junctions from crossing wires.
AI.method: SINA is a fully automated pipeline integrating: (1) deep learning for robust component detection, (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, (3) OCR for component reference designator extraction, (4) VLM for reliable reference designator assignment, and (5) dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate connections from intersections. Graph isomorphism validates generated netlist correctness.
AI.result: Overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics.
AI.conclusion: SINA effectively bridges the gap between visual circuit schematic representations and machine-readable formats, enabling simulation, verification, and database construction for AI-driven analog and mixed-signal EDA.

title: ICDepth: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Video Depth Estimation via In-Context Conditioning
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://xuanhuahe.github.io/ICDepth/
summary: Monocular video depth estimation requires temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios, yet existing methods struggle to achieve all three simultaneously. Discriminative models excel at per-frame accuracy but suffer from temporal drift due to limited context windows, while generative methods improve consistency and generalization at the cost of extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack of geometric precision. In response to these issues, we introduce \textbf{ICDepth}, a framework that adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), leveraging their rich spatial-temporal priors. To address key challenges in transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction, we propose: (1)~\textbf{SAND-Attention}, which ensures precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and enforces unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2)~\textbf{SRFM}, which injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. ICDepth achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency, trained on only 0.8M frames ($6$--$13\times$ less than competing generative methods), while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.

AI.tldr: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for monocular video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning, achieving SOTA results with only 0.8M training frames (6-13x less than competitors) through SAND-Attention for spatial-temporal alignment and SRFM for geometric precision.
AI.motivation: Existing video depth estimation methods fail to achieve temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization simultaneously. Discriminative models suffer temporal drift from limited context, while generative methods lack geometric precision and require extensive training data (10M+ samples).
AI.method: ICDepth adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for dense prediction via In-Context Conditioning (ICC). It introduces (1) SAND-Attention with shared RoPE for spatial-temporal alignment and unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination, and (2) SRFM that injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to improve geometric precision.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency (trained on only 0.8M frames, 6-13x less than competing generative methods), with strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: ICDepth demonstrates that leveraging pre-trained video diffusion priors with carefully designed attention mechanisms enables efficient, geometrically precise, and temporally consistent video depth estimation without requiring massive training datasets.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework maps 452 benchmarks into O*NET work activities and BIAN banking domains, using multiplicative weighting (discrimination × coverage × recency) and Elo-based scoring to produce work-activity and business-domain scores without raw-score normalization, demonstrated on 288 models from 25 organizations as of June 2026.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize for aggregate performance and fail to capture domain-specific cognitive demands of financial-services work (e.g., compliance reasoning, multi-turn customer interactions), leading to mismatches between leaderboard rankings and actual task requirements in banking contexts.
AI.method: 452 benchmarks are taxonomically organized into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregated into 38 BIAN banking business domains. A multiplicative weighting (discrimination × coverage × recency) computed over a rolling model window prioritizes benchmarks that separate top models, are widely reported, and remain active. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, yielding cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw-score normalization; business-domain scores are weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organizations as of June 2026.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reproducible approach for financial institutions to address model selection and governance challenges by aligning benchmark evaluation with specific work activities and business domains relevant to financial services.

title: HTTP REST API Structure Learning
summary: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

AI.tldr: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models API endpoint structure and behavior from network traffic to detect malicious activity, achieving 82.07% recall and 87.24% F1-score, with 100% detection when combined with signature-based rules.
AI.motivation: APIs are widely used but pose significant security risks; existing approaches rely on predefined rules or documentation which may be incomplete or unavailable.
AI.method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) is an unsupervised anomaly detection method that learns API endpoint structure and behavior directly from network traffic without requiring predefined rules or documentation.
AI.result: Average recall of 82.07%, F1-score of 87.24%; approaches effectiveness of full API documentation; combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS achieves 100% detection.
AI.conclusion: HRAL is effective in real-world, partially documented API environments and serves as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multimodal framework combining protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs (drug, disease, miRNA, lncRNA) for cold-start PPI prediction, using a bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating module to outperform baselines in novel-old and novel-novel settings.
AI.motivation: Cold-start PPI prediction (where candidate proteins have no observed PPI edges during training) is challenging because topology-based models lose useful context, yet accurate prediction in this setting is critical for functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development.
AI.method: The method combines (1) region-aware protein sequence encoding with structural context, (2) graph attention encoders over four KG modalities (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA), (3) a bridge reconstruction objective to regularize graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and (4) a pair-level gating module to adaptively integrate sequence and graph evidence for each protein pair.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC on two benchmark datasets under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal fusion of sequence and diverse biomedical KG embeddings with adaptive gating and reconstruction regularization effectively addresses the cold-start PPI prediction problem where topology alone is insufficient.

title: Structure-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has demonstrated remarkable potential in novel view synthesis. In contrast to small-scale scenes, large-scale scenes inevitably contain sparsely observed regions with excessively sparse initial points. In this case, supervising Gaussians initialized from low-frequency sparse points with high-frequency images often induces uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, degrading both efficiency and quality. Intuitively, this issue can be mitigated with scheduling strategies, which can be categorized into two paradigms: modulating target signal frequency via densification and modulating sampling frequency via image resolution. However, previous scheduling strategies are primarily hardcoded, failing to perceive the convergence behavior of scene frequency. To address this, we reframe the scene reconstruction problem from the perspective of signal structure recovery and propose SIG, a novel scheduler that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies. Specifically, we derive the average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, and then regulate the training image resolution and the Gaussian densification process based on scene frequency convergence. Furthermore, we introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians, which leverage the spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization. Our framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training, achieving state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes. The code is available at: https://github.com/weiyixue999/Signal_Structure_Aware_Gaussian

AI.tldr: SIG is a novel scheduler for 3D Gaussian Splatting that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies by regulating training image resolution and densification based on scene frequency convergence, plus Sphere-Constrained Gaussians for spatial priors, achieving SOTA in large-scale scenes.
AI.motivation: Large-scale scenes contain sparsely observed regions with sparse initial points, causing uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives when supervising low-frequency Gaussians with high-frequency images. Previous hardcoded scheduling strategies fail to perceive scene frequency convergence behavior.
AI.method: (1) Derives average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations to regulate training image resolution and Gaussian densification based on scene frequency convergence. (2) Introduces Sphere-Constrained Gaussians that leverage spatial priors of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training for large-scale scene reconstruction.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav introduces a unified on-policy framework with hindsight reasoning to bridge the semantic supervision gap in Vision-Language Navigation, achieving competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks using fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN causes semantic mismatch between the agent's visual stream and original language instructions due to trajectory deviation from expert demonstrations, creating a need to align instructions with exploratory journeys.
AI.method: Phi-Nav operates in a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes path-level hindsight instruction from collected visual observations, 3) a second imitation pass treating the synthesized pair as additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is necessary in VLN, and Phi-Nav effectively enables training embodied agents with limited data by transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals.

title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
comment: TestEvo-Bench leaderboard and data explorer are hosted at https://www.testevo-bench.com
summary:
Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

AI.tldr: TestEvo-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating test automation agents on test-code co-evolution tasks (generation & update) using real commits, execution-grounded metrics, and temporal splits to reduce data leakage.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks isolate tests from code changes and rely on static metadata without verifying executability or semantic relevance, making it hard to evaluate if agents understand how code changes propagate into test suites.
AI.method: Mined 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. Tasks are anchored to real commit history with environment configuration for execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score). Live benchmark with timestamp-based temporal splits to prevent data leakage.
AI.result: SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent with strong LLMs) achieve up to 77.5% success on test generation and 74.6% on test update, but performance drops on recent tasks and under limited per-task cost.
AI.conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a more realistic, execution-verified evaluation for test automation agents, revealing that current agents still struggle with recent tasks and cost-constrained settings.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance mechanism for LLM training that uses hot-swapping (replacing failed nodes with spares without job termination), enabled by off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing and communicator reconstruction, achieving zero overhead during failure-free execution and recovery under 40 seconds on up to 512 GPUs with 65B parameter models.
AI.motivation: Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms for LLM training either incur non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency under permanent node failures, creating a tradeoff that DeadPool aims to simultaneously address.
AI.method: DeadPool introduces (1) an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy that overlaps with computation (zero overhead), and (2) a communicator reconstruction protocol that hot-swaps failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime without terminating the job.
AI.result: Evaluated on up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B parameters, DeadPool achieves zero checkpoint overhead and hot-swapping recovery completes in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost, demonstrating effective Pareto-optimal fault tolerance for large-scale LLM training.

title: LASER: A Corrective Lens for LVLMs via Visual Attention Preservation and Sink Suppression
comment: The 19th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV 2026)
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit strong reasoning ability but suffer from visual forgetting during long-horizon decoding, where attention progressively drifts away from visual evidence. Existing methods largely treat this issue as a late-stage attention decay problem or attempt to mitigate it through heuristic reminders or post-hoc attention lifting. Through systematic empirical analysis, we find that performance degradation under visual forgetting is largely driven by two overlooked factors: early-stage attention decay disrupts evidence acquisition, and attention concentration on a subset of task-irrelevant visual sink tokens. Motivated by these insights, we propose LASER, a post-training framework that regulates both the visual attention trajectory and intra-visual token attention distribution during reasoning. Technically, LASER introduces two complementary rewards: a Visual Grounding Reward, which encourages the model to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens throughout decoding, and a Sink Suppression Reward, which penalizes excessive attention concentration on visual sink tokens. Together, these rewards preserve early-stage grounding while preventing attention collapse onto uninformative regions. Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that LASER consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.

AI.tldr: LASER is a post-training framework that addresses visual forgetting in LVLMs by using two complementary rewards: Visual Grounding Reward (maintains attention on salient visual tokens) and Sink Suppression Reward (penalizes attention on task-irrelevant visual sink tokens). It outperforms baselines across eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Visual forgetting during long-horizon decoding in LVLMs causes attention to drift away from visual evidence. Existing methods treat this as late-stage attention decay or use heuristic reminders, but overlook two key factors: early-stage attention decay disrupting evidence acquisition, and attention concentration on task-irrelevant visual sink tokens.
AI.method: LASER introduces two complementary rewards: (1) Visual Grounding Reward to maintain attention on semantically salient visual tokens throughout decoding, and (2) Sink Suppression Reward to penalize excessive attention concentration on visual sink tokens. Together they preserve early-stage grounding and prevent attention collapse.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that LASER consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating attention-aware training as an effective remedy for visual forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Attention-aware post-training with dual rewards (visual grounding + sink suppression) effectively mitigates visual forgetting in LVLMs by regulating both the visual attention trajectory and intra-visual token attention distribution during reasoning.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind is a dual-loop framework for repository-level vulnerability reproduction that learns reusable high-level strategies via SFT and milestone-based GRPO, achieving 84.5% pass rate with GPT-5.5 and transferring across multiple LLM executors.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents for vulnerability reproduction fail not due to incorrect execution steps but due to wrong strategic choices (e.g., which input grammar to infer, which path to trace). Strategy—compact, concrete, and reusable—is identified as the right learning unit, but prior work optimizes full action trajectories which are too sparse and task-specific.
AI.method: Mastermind uses a dual-loop architecture: (1) a trainable planner loop that learns reusable strategies via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and milestone-based GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), trained independently of the executor; (2) an experience loop that maintains task-local strategy records to guide subsequent attempts. The planner is decoupled from the frozen executor, enabling strategy transfer across different LLMs.
AI.result: On CyberGym (260 training, 200 held-out tasks), Mastermind with GPT-5.5 achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner boosts GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM~5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents, enabling multiple frozen executors to benefit from a single trained planner without modifying their generation capabilities.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM is a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint (unimodal) datasets by aligning them in a shared latent space, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and revealing biologically consistent links in autism spectrum disorder.
AI.motivation: Most large-scale datasets are unimodal (providing either neuroimaging or genetics data), yet understanding brain structure-genetic interactions is key for neuropsychiatric disorders. There is a need to leverage existing unimodal repositories to study cross-modal interactions without requiring paired data.
AI.method: CALM aligns imaging and genetics modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability, enabling interpretable pathway-ROI associations from completely disjoint populations.
AI.result: When trained on unimodal datasets, CALM generalizes to unseen paired datasets, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. It demonstrates stability of learned associations against a paired baseline. Experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, consistent with established literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

title: Consistent Scene Understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting via Multi-Cue Mask Refinement
summary: Reliable instance-level scene understanding is a fundamental prerequisite for object-level interactions and high-fidelity 3D representations. While current methods often leverage 2D foundation segmentation models to obtain these priors, their 2D-centric design typically yields fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across different views. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework that produces consistent 2D instance masks to guide the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) feature fields. Our framework consists of three main stages. (1) Multi-Cue Extraction that generates synergistic semantic, geometric, and structural priors from input images. (2) Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging process that consolidates fragmented masks using a composite merge score derived from semantic, depth, and edge cues. (3) Cross-View Mask Matching that establishes globally consistent identity assignments across all viewpoints. By transforming viewpoint-specific segments into coherent 3D primitives, our approach enables stable 3D instance segmentation and effective downstream editing tasks. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves cross-view consistency and segmentation stability over existing baselines while maintaining high-fidelity photometric reconstruction.

AI.tldr: A framework using multi-cue extraction, guided mask merging, and cross-view mask matching to produce consistent 2D instance masks for optimizing 3DGS feature fields, improving cross-view consistency and segmentation stability.
AI.motivation: Current methods using 2D foundation segmentation models produce fragmented masks and inconsistent predictions across different views, hindering reliable instance-level scene understanding for object-level interactions and 3D representations.
AI.method: Three-stage framework: (1) Multi-Cue Extraction generating synergistic semantic, geometric, and structural priors; (2) Multi-Cue-Guided Mask Merging consolidating fragmented masks via composite merge scores; (3) Cross-View Mask Matching establishing globally consistent identity assignments across viewpoints.
AI.result: Significant improvement in cross-view consistency and segmentation stability over existing baselines while maintaining high-fidelity photometric reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Transforming viewpoint-specific segments into coherent 3D primitives enables stable 3D instance segmentation and effective downstream editing tasks.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text using Blender, featuring a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, layered scene protocol, and runtime inspection tools, along with 4DBuildBench for evaluating visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for text-to-3D focus on static scenes; dynamic 4D scenes (liquids, particles, rigid bodies, articulated motion) remain unexplored despite their value for editable content and physics-grounded training data, with key challenges being joint coordination of spatial layout, physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting, and the difficulty of verifying motion correctness from rendered video.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow for fixed ordered construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite to catch mechanism failures not visible in rendered images.
AI.result: SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines on the introduced 4DBuildBench benchmark, which assesses both visual fidelity and physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent approach with structured verification and runtime inspection effectively addresses the challenges of generating dynamic 4D scenes from text, enabling physically consistent and editable procedural content.

title: Beyond Pixel Diffs: Benchmarking Image Change Captioning for Web UI Visual Regression Testing
summary: Visual regression testing (VRT) is a standard quality assurance step in modern software release pipelines. On every change, it re-renders user interface (UI) screenshots, compares each one against an approved baseline image, and routes any detected difference to a human reviewer who decides whether it is an intended update or an unintended regression. A widely used approach, especially in open-source and continuous-integration pipelines, is pixel-level comparison, which is semantically blind and treats rendering noise and genuine defects identically, producing large volumes of false positives that force developers and testers to spend substantial time and effort manually reviewing flagged differences at every release cycle. Industry tools apply machine learning to VRT, but lack public evaluation. More critically, no dataset or benchmark exists to support natural language descriptions of UI changes, a capability that tells testers what changed in words instead of leaving them to interpret a binary flag or a highlighted region. To address the gap, we propose a new task, Web UI Image Change Captioning (WUICC), which sits at the intersection of VRT and image difference captioning (IDC), and release WUICC-bench, its first dataset and benchmark for the task. We evaluate eleven representative IDC methods, together with two zero-shot general-purpose LLMs. We find that: (1) these methods tend to struggle in the Web UI domain due to its layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes, and (2) yet the trained methods already suppress non-meaningful visual noise far more selectively than the pixel-level comparison VRT relies on, providing a solid foundation for future domain-specific research.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Web UI Image Change Captioning (WUICC), a new task combining visual regression testing and image difference captioning, along with a benchmark dataset (WUICC-bench). Evaluations show existing methods struggle with Web UI domains but outperform pixel-level VRT in selectively suppressing non-meaningful visual noise.
AI.motivation: Current pixel-level visual regression testing generates excessive false positives by treating rendering noise and genuine defects identically, forcing manual review of every flagged difference. No dataset or benchmark exists for natural language descriptions of UI changes.
AI.method: The authors define a new task (WUICC) at the intersection of VRT and IDC, release a new dataset and benchmark (WUICC-bench), and evaluate 11 representative IDC methods plus two zero-shot LLMs on the task.
AI.result: Existing IDC methods and LLMs struggle in the Web UI domain due to layout diversity, dense text, and fine-grained changes. However, trained methods suppress non-meaningful visual noise more selectively than pixel-level VRT.
AI.conclusion: The WUICC task and benchmark address a critical gap in VRT by enabling natural language descriptions of UI changes, and current findings highlight the need for domain-specific research.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework using a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to jointly track fast-varying wireless channels and slow-varying hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers, achieving robust and lower channel estimation error than conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. Existing conventional compensators fail to effectively handle these impairments.
AI.method: The method uses an RGRU to model intra-slot hardware impairment memory. A two-timescale Bayesian framework assigns a fast-varying Markov prior to sparse channels and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior to impairment network parameters. A multi-slot factor graph is formulated; inter-slot messages have closed-form updates, while intra-slot is partitioned into a channel tracking module (Turbo-OAMP for sparse estimation) and an impairments calibration module (DAMP for parameter updates), exchanging information via expectation propagation (EP).
AI.result: Simulations show the proposed MP-TTBDL framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error compared to conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.conclusion: The two-timescale Bayesian deep learning approach effectively separates and jointly tracks channel and hardware impairment dynamics, outperforming conventional methods.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: This paper studies world-model correctors for repairing failed planning graphs in persistent agent workflows, proposing WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair) which outperforms standard engineering approaches by identifying and repairing only the causal subgraph that propagates errors.
AI.motivation: As agent planning scales to long persistent workflows (thousands+ steps), failures occur inside large planning graphs rather than isolated predictions. Replanning entire graphs after each mistake is computationally unrealistic and degrades performance due to large context budgets and irrelevant symptom exposure.
AI.method: Compares two families of correctors: (1) Engineering LLM correctors that scan nodes/edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. (2) WM-SAR, which works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies nodes and edges that re-amplify error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM for repair.
AI.result: Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and provides the LLM a cleaner repair target.
AI.conclusion: WM-SAR offers an efficient alternative to full-graph replay for error correction in long-horizon agent planning, focusing on causal subgraph repair rather than broad symptom scanning.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is the first tool to measure complexity in both prompt and code layers of LLM-integrated applications, using a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism. After evaluating 52 metrics against 118 components, only 10 survived significance testing, with 7 new prompt-layer metrics (measuring structural breadth) outperforming traditional code metrics. Prompt complexity proves to be an independent dimension of overall complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics only operate at the code level, overlooking the behavioral logic that originates in the prompt layer of LLM-integrated applications, where much of the runtime behavior actually resides.
AI.method: (1) Developed HECATE with Prompt-as-Specification formalism (Hoare-logic-inspired). (2) Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, generating 52 candidate metrics. (3) Evaluated metrics against 118 components from 18 open-source repos using maintenance activity from version history as proxy. (4) Discarded metrics losing significance after accounting for code size. (5) Final validation on 20 components from 6 held-out repos.
AI.result: Only 10 metrics survived: 7 new structural breadth metrics (tallying LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates), 1 conventional metric (RFC) with similar breadth character, and 2 (Halstead N and V) as residual size effects. Prompt-layer metrics retained significance even with strongest code-level metric as covariate.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity is an independent, significant dimension of complexity in LLM-integrated applications that existing code-level metrics fail to capture. The two best-performing metrics generalize beyond the training set, supporting their practical utility.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) with compressed communication, achieving more elegant design and better regret bounds than existing OGD-type methods, particularly in the bandit setting.
AI.motivation: Existing D-OCO algorithms with compressed communication are all variants of OGD, while the best algorithms for exact communication are FTRL-based. This gap motivates the need for FTRL-type algorithms that can handle communication compression, offering simpler and more effective solutions.
AI.method: Two FTRL-type algorithms are proposed for D-OCO with compressed communication. The first algorithm addresses the full-information setting and matches existing regret bounds. The second algorithm targets the bandit setting. The key technique leverages the dual update mechanism of FTRL to seamlessly integrate average consensus with communication compression.
AI.result: The first algorithm matches existing regret bounds in the full-information setting. The second algorithm significantly improves both regret bounds and communication costs compared to existing algorithms in the bandit setting.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms are shown to be more elegant than OGD-type ones for D-OCO with compressed communication, offering simpler algorithmic design and theoretical analysis while achieving superior performance, especially in bandit settings.

title: ReQuest: Rethinking-based Question-Aware Frame Selection for Long-Form Video QA
summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced video understanding, yet long-form video QA remains challenging under fixed input token budgets, where uniform sampling can be inefficient for evidence localization. We propose ReQuest , an uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection pipeline that aligns question intent with relevant video content through selective computation. ReQuest integrates (i) a lightweight question-aware selector distilled from MLLM-generated supervision, (ii) Re-thinking Routing that triggers additional inference only when the model is uncertain with a length-adaptive criterion, and (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression that selects temporally diverse frames while adjusting spacing based on question difficulty. As a plug-andplay method, ReQuest improves long-video QA without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying MLLM. Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, with particularly strong improvements in medium and long video regimes.

AI.tldr: ReQuest is an uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection pipeline that improves long-form video QA by selectively aligning question intent with relevant video content, using a lightweight selector, re-thinking routing, and adaptive NMS, without modifying the underlying MLLM.
AI.motivation: Long-form video QA under fixed input token budgets is challenging because uniform sampling is inefficient for evidence localization. The paper aims to bridge the gap between question intent and relevant video content without modifying or fine-tuning the underlying MLLM.
AI.method: ReQuest integrates three components: (i) a lightweight question-aware selector distilled from MLLM-generated supervision, (ii) Re-thinking Routing that triggers additional inference only when the model is uncertain using a length-adaptive criterion, and (iii) uncertainty-guided adaptive non-maximum suppression for selecting temporally diverse frames with spacing adjusted by question difficulty.
AI.result: Experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench show consistent accuracy gains with competitive computational cost, with particularly strong improvements in medium and long video regimes.
AI.conclusion: ReQuest effectively improves long-video QA as a plug-and-play method without requiring MLLM modification or fine-tuning, demonstrating that uncertainty-driven, question-adaptive keyframe selection is a viable strategy for evidence localization under token constraints.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample.
