The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented SLM framework using formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop is proposed for ontology construction. The system validates implications via a retrieval-grounded oracle and supports various knowledge checks. In a rare ataxia domain, it achieves relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and implication F1 of 0.22-0.30, with ablations showing incidence judgments improve closure-based scores but identifying positive pairs remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Ontology construction faces challenges in deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations are valid. Language models can propose structures from text but often produce unsupported or inconsistent outputs, motivating a framework that integrates symbolic verification to improve reliability.
AI.method: A retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework is combined with formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop. Starting from seed attributes, FCA generates implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle validates each implication, returns counterexamples, and supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals.
AI.result: In a rare ataxia setting from Orphadata resources, 10-seed runs achieve relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. Lower implication scores are due to strict evaluation where one missed or extra relation affects multiple judgments. Ablations show incidence judgments improve closure-based scores, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively combines retrieval-augmented SLMs with FCA-based symbolic verification for knowledge expansion, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains a key challenge even under fixed conditions.

title: Search-based Testing of Vision Language Models for In-Car Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at the Industry Track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: In the automotive domain, in-car scene understanding (ISU) enables the detection of safety-critical events, such as driver distraction, and supports drivers or passengers by analyzing the in-car scene and adapting the environment (e.g., ambient lighting). The industry is increasingly exploring vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret camera-recorded in-car scenes and extract information for downstream reasoning tasks. However, VLMs may generate incomplete, erroneous, or misleading scene descriptions, highlighting the need for systematic testing. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, particularly in early design stages. In this paper, we present ISU-Test, an automated testing approach that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate ISU systems. By framing testing as an optimization problem and systematically modifying scene parameters, our method generates diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations. We evaluate ISU-Test on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two case studies: question answering and captioning, comparing against randomized scenario generation. Results show that ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage.

AI.tldr: ISU-Test is an automated testing approach for in-car scene understanding systems that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate vision-language models, achieving up to 10x higher failure rates and 3.6x higher failure coverage compared to randomized baselines.
AI.motivation: VLMs used for in-car scene understanding may generate incomplete or erroneous descriptions, yet systematic testing is hindered by the high cost and scalability issues of collecting real in-vehicle data, especially in early design stages.
AI.method: ISU-Test combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing, framing testing as an optimization problem to systematically modify scene parameters and generate diverse in-car scenarios.
AI.result: ISU-Test outperforms randomized scenario generation, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage across question answering and captioning tasks on both industrial prototype and open-source VLMs.
AI.conclusion: Search-based testing with rendered scenes is an effective and scalable approach for systematically evaluating VLM-based ISU systems, significantly outperforming randomized baselines.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a physics-informed state routing model for day-ahead wind power forecasting that combines a site-calibrated physical prior with latent operating-state modeling and state-aware correction, achieving accurate and robust performance across 20+ real-world datasets in full-shot and zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Wind power forecasting is critical for power system operation, but existing physical models generalize poorly across farms, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations (e.g., shutdowns, curtailment).
AI.method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) Physical Prior Estimator with site-conditioned monotonic warping and a shared physical power curve under a physical upper-bound constraint; (2) Latent State Encoder for modeling operating-state embeddings; (3) State-aware Power Corrector using knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on over 20 real-world datasets demonstrate accuracy and robustness of UniWind.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively decouples meteorological effects from operational state deviations and generalizes across farms, outperforming both purely physical and purely data-driven approaches.

title: InterCMDM: Block-Causal Diffusion for Autoregressive Human Interaction Generation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026, Project website: https://yu1ut.com/InterCMDM-HP/
summary: Text-conditioned human interaction generation must capture both long-range temporal causality within each individual and tightly coupled coordination between partners. Existing interaction diffusion models typically denoise full sequences using bidirectional attention, which obscures causality and hinders streaming and long-horizon generation. Autoregressive alternatives enforce causality but often suffer from temporal drift, leading to coordination degradation and unstable interaction dynamics over time. We propose InterCMDM, a block-causal latent diffusion framework for autoregressive two-person interaction generation. InterCMDM introduces a Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer that maintains separate causal streams for each person while modeling inter-person dependencies via unified dual-stream attention with multi-task attention masks. These masks unify interaction modeling within a single attention mechanism and support diverse coordination behaviors, including simultaneous actions, reactive responses, leader-follower dynamics, and independent motion. By training a single model across these mask configurations as a form of data augmentation, InterCMDM enables controllable interaction generation by simply selecting the desired attention mask at inference time. Finally, a block-wise diffusion objective enables stable latent rollout over long sequences without repeated decode-encode cycles. InterCMDM achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X, improving text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity.

AI.tldr: InterCMDM is a block-causal latent diffusion framework for autoregressive two-person interaction generation that uses Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer with multi-task attention masks to model both intra-person causality and inter-person dependencies, achieving state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X.
AI.motivation: Existing interaction diffusion models use bidirectional attention that obscures causality and hinders streaming/long-horizon generation, while autoregressive alternatives suffer from temporal drift, coordination degradation, and unstable interaction dynamics over time.
AI.method: Proposes InterCMDM with: (1) Dual-Stream Causal Diffusion Transformer maintaining separate causal streams per person; (2) multi-task attention masks unifying inter-person modeling within single attention, supporting simultaneous actions, reactive responses, leader-follower dynamics, and independent motion; (3) training across mask configurations as data augmentation for controllable generation via mask selection at inference; (4) block-wise diffusion objective for stable latent rollout without repeated decode-encode cycles.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterHuman and Inter-X datasets, with improvements in text-motion alignment, realism, and long-horizon continuity.
AI.conclusion: Block-causal latent diffusion with multi-task attention masks effectively addresses causality, coordination, and temporal drift challenges in two-person interaction generation, enabling controllable and long-horizon interaction synthesis.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models encode a latent representation of denoising progress (timestep) in their residual streams, which can be extracted via probes and manipulated to modulate model confidence and entropy.
AI.motivation: To understand how Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) internally represent and utilize denoising progress information, given that they are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep unlike standard diffusion-based approaches.
AI.method: Probing across layers to extract timestep-related signals from residual stream activations; steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep to modulate denoising progress; analyzing the geometric structure of the identified representation.
AI.result: DLMs encode a reliably decodable latent representation of denoising progress; steering along the identified low-dimensional subspace systematically modulates model confidence and entropy in a predictable manner; the representation exhibits structured and interpretable geometric properties in activation space.
AI.conclusion: DLMs internally represent denoising progress despite lacking explicit timestep conditioning, and this signal can be extracted and manipulated, revealing interpretable structure in how these models process diffusion information.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Coding agents require human oversight, and applying traditional software engineering constraints (access control, network policies, coding conventions) to agents is cheaper and more effective than recent agentic scaffolding. A controlled experiment showed backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained) to 90.9% (constrained substrate + tools), with largest gains in Python (weak guarantees) and principles extensible to Rust.
AI.motivation: Human oversight is the bottleneck for coding agents; unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review costly. The authors aim to show that traditional software engineering management methods transfer effectively to coding agents and are more cost-efficient than current agentic scaffolding approaches.
AI.method: Start-to-end system sketch based on traditional engineering management principles (access control, network policies, coding conventions enforced by tooling). Controlled experiment: small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors, comparing unconstrained vs. constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI tool.
AI.result: Recall of backdoor detection rose from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus tools). Substrate and tools contributed independently to the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Constraining coding agents via traditional engineering management principles is cheaper (in tokens) than recent agentic scaffolding and significantly improves oversight. Gains are largest in languages with weak guarantees (like Python) but principles extend to stronger-guarantee languages like Rust.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM pre-training that uses first-moment-based sparsification (derived from AdamS's statistics) to achieve up to 99% sparsity without quality loss, reducing wall-clock time by up to 43.3% (Llama-500M) and achieving 3.26× speedup per step (Llama-1.8B) on 32 GH200 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Communication cost dominates LLM pre-training under data-parallel and sharded training, and existing sparsification methods are unstable for Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, while quantization has fundamental bit-width limits and runtime overhead.
AI.method: SCAPE leverages the stability of AdamS's first-moment to construct masks from first-moment-based statistics (not raw gradients), partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, delays mask usage by one step for overlap with computation, and reconstructs second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer to avoid an extra collective.
AI.result: On GPT-345M and Llama-500M, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy at 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, it reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 43.3%; for Llama-1.8B, it achieves up to 3.26× speedup per step vs. dense AdamS, all on 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE enables aggressive sparsification (up to 99%) for Adam-style optimizers without quality degradation, effectively reducing communication overhead in large-scale LLM pre-training while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS.

title: RTE-FM-Dehazer: Radiative Transfer Equation Inspired Flow Matching for Real-World Image Dehazing
summary: Single-image dehazing aims to recover a clear scene from a hazy image and is generally formulated as an image-to-image translation task; however, it faces two limitations. Its performance depends heavily on the haze-formation priors embedded in the model. Prevailing methods adopt the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), whose assumptions of single scattering and homogeneous media are often violated, leading to residual haze and color drift. Moreover, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and existing synthesis approaches fail to reproduce the full complexity of natural haze. To address these issues, we present RTE-FM-Dehazer, a novel dehazing approach, together with a scalable data pipeline. Unlike the ASM, the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) jointly accounts for both scattering and absorption, naturally accommodating the non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media that characterize real hazy scenes. Motivated by the structural similarity between the RTE diffusion-absorption term and the ODE in flow matching, we introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, to steer the flow matching trajectory at each step. Next, leveraging modern vision-language models, we build an automated pipeline and release P-HAZE, a dataset of 50000 realistic hazy/clear pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates artifacts like residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RTE-FM-Dehazer is a single-image dehazing method that replaces the traditional Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM) with the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to better handle non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media. It uses a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from RTE to guide flow matching, and introduces P-HAZE, a 50K realistic hazy/clear dataset generated via an automated vision-language pipeline. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on five real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image dehazing methods rely on the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), which assumes single scattering and homogeneous media—assumptions often violated in real haze, causing residual haze and color drift. Additionally, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and synthetic datasets fail to capture natural haze complexity.
AI.method: The authors replace ASM with the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to jointly model scattering and absorption in non-homogeneous media. They derive a diffusion-absorption regularizer from a reduced RTE, exploiting its structural similarity to the ODE in flow matching, to guide the flow matching trajectory. They also build an automated data pipeline using vision-language models to generate P-HAZE, a 50K realistic hazy/clear dataset.
AI.result: RTE-FM-Dehazer trained solely on P-HAZE effectively removes artifacts (residual haze, color drift), exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Replacing ASM with RTE and combining it with flow matching regularization, along with a scalable synthetic data pipeline producing realistic haze, yields superior dehazing performance and generalization across diverse real-world scenarios.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (risk discovery, combinatorial safety case generation, adaptive execution with evidence-grounded verification) to evaluate safety across four production agent frameworks, achieving 93.9% attack success rates and producing Vera-Bench with 1600 safety cases across 124 risk categories.
AI.motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed safety violations and hard-coded evaluation rules, which are costly to extend as agents evolve. There is a need for an automated, scalable, and maintainable approach to discover and test emerging safety risks in increasingly autonomous agent systems.
AI.method: Vera instantiates software engineering testing principles via a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration to discover and structure risks into taxonomies; (2) combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases with concrete goals, initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution using isolated sandboxes, a control agent for multi-turn steering, and evidence-grounded verifiers based on environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), Vera revealed substantial safety weaknesses with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. The released Vera-Bench comprises 1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories and three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. Vera demonstrates that automated, combinatorial, and evidence-grounded approaches can effectively replace costly expert-designed testing.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP recovers the training domain mixtures of fine-tuned models from their weights by interpolating between base and fine-tuned models via model merging, extracting geometric features, and mapping them to domain proportions.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are publicly released but their training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an access asymmetry where researchers can study models but cannot characterize the global composition of training corpora.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned models via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory, exposing geometric footprints of training data in weight space. It then extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP effectively recovers training domain mixtures from model weights alone, outperforming existing methods like membership inference, and addresses the critical transparency gap in foundation model release practices.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench is a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding that evaluates not only answer correctness but also when models should answer, defer judgment, or raise alerts, revealing significant performance gaps between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making across 22 datasets and 5,419 QA instances.
AI.motivation: Existing medical video benchmarks only assess answer correctness, not the timing of responses. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide both what to predict and when to answer, defer, or alert, creating a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements.
AI.method: MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets with 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive), restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows, supports single-turn and streaming evaluation, introduces a proactive monitoring setting for clinically relevant alert timing, and evaluates via responsiveness and post-evidence stability metrics.
AI.result: Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models show a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings.
AI.conclusion: MedStreamBench addresses a critical gap in medical video understanding by evaluating temporal decision-making behavior, demonstrating that current models struggle significantly with time-aware reasoning tasks required for real clinical deployment.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a novel multimodal AI framework integrating Memory-SAM, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL, and RAG to improve TCM tongue diagnosis, outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on the new MedTCM dataset using the TDEU evaluation metric.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and reproducibility issues; multimodal AI application is hindered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, plus the lack of large-scale standardized datasets.
AI.method: A three-stage architecture: (1) training-free Memory-SAM for robust tongue segmentation; (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue diagnosis generation; (3) Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Introduces MedTCM dataset and TDEU evaluation metric.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively bridges the semantic gap in multimodal TCM diagnosis, demonstrating superior clinical accuracy validated by the novel TDEU metric on the MedTCM dataset.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes model merging as a probabilistic inference problem using product-of-experts (PoE) with energy-based models, identifies that existing methods impose inappropriate Gaussian assumptions on residuals, and proposes a heavy-tailed Cauchy expert design that better matches observed residual behavior and achieves SOTA results.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which provide limited guidance for statistically scoring the usefulness of task-specific update directions across tasks during merging.
AI.method: Formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) framework where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over merged parameters; identifies that existing methods correspond to implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals; proposes heavy-tailed PoE based on Cauchy experts to better capture the observed heavy-tailed residual behavior.
AI.result: Empirical findings show residuals are often heavy-tailed, mismatching Gaussian assumptions. The proposed Cauchy expert design yields a provably convergent inference procedure and achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks and architectures.
AI.conclusion: Model merging can be effectively reformulated as probabilistic inference under PoE, and heavy-tailed (Cauchy) expert designs are better suited than Gaussian-based designs for capturing the statistical properties of residuals in practice.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D plant phenotyping framework powered by 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) that replaces traditional COLMAP-style sparse initialization with feed-forward geometric recovery, reducing reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high quality across 26 plant sequences with smartphone-captured multi-view images.
AI.motivation: Conventional 3D plant phenotyping is procedure-complicated, low-throughput, and fragile due to extensive multi-view imaging, complex reconstruction pipelines, and additional geometry-to-phenotype extraction steps. These issues are amplified in low-cost smartphone-based data acquisition with limited view overlap and self-occlusion.
AI.method: The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement, and performs 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation for phenotypic measurement.
AI.result: Across 26 plant sequences, the framework reduces average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. A cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations was constructed.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement, enabled by 3D Foundation Models.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions for evaluating LLMs on aviation-specific knowledge. Current models (best: 82.7%) fall well short of the expert reference (~95%), revealing a persistent gap for safe deployment in aviation operations.
AI.motivation: General-purpose benchmarks fail to measure whether LLMs reason safely and correctly about aviation-specific operational knowledge, which is consequential given the high-stakes, regulated nature of the domain.
AI.method: 300 multiple choice questions were drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering ground operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge, and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by aviation practitioners. Models were evaluated using the Inspect framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol.
AI.result: The strongest model (released 2026) achieved 82.7%, improving from ~75% in early 2025. Expert reference from a conference survey of aviation professionals was ~95%. A substantial and persistent gap below expert-level reliability remains.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: Proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, designed for beginning graduate students.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, accessible bridge from classical sampling methods to modern diffusion models for graduate students with probability background but no prior knowledge of SDEs or diffusion models.
AI.method: Layered exposition with core definitions and identities proven fully, representative estimates under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems with proof roadmaps.
AI.result: A pedagogical framework that traces a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers including error analysis and inference-time control.
AI.conclusion: These notes serve as a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models for sampling, suitable for beginning graduate students.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for LDCT denoising that integrates anatomical-prior-guided conditioning, residual frequency-domain decoupling, and time-step-decoupling denoising to outperform existing methods in image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and downstream task utility.
AI.motivation: Low-dose CT reduces radiation but introduces noise, artifacts, and texture degradation that obscure anatomy. Existing diffusion models for LDCT denoising lack sufficient anatomical guidance, frequency-dependent recovery, and adaptive reverse-process modeling.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT is a multi-stage diffusion model with three key modules: (1) Anatomical-Prior-Guided Conditioning (APGC) for extracting structural guidance from LDCT; (2) Residual Frequency-Domain Decoupling Stage (RFDDS) for frequency-aware representations; (3) Time-Step-Decoupling Denoising Decoder (TD3) that distributes these representations across reverse-diffusion stages for progressive anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT benchmarks, ProSAC-CT outperforms representative methods in image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation, with better preservation of boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream classification on Mayo-2020 confirms retained task-relevant anatomical information.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT effectively addresses key limitations of prior diffusion-based LDCT denoising by incorporating progressive spectral-anatomical guidance and stage-adaptive denoising, demonstrating practical clinical utility for low-dose CT denoising.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM addresses spectral bias in physics-informed machine learning by using an additive weight initialization that shifts the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity, avoiding variance amplification. Two variants (FS-PIELM-L and FS-PIELM-G) are tested on seven benchmarks, with the linear variant achieving improvements of 1-5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM methods.
AI.motivation: Solving PDEs with high-frequency solutions is challenging in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias, where neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency components. Existing scaling-based weight initialization methods amplify variance, hindering performance on high-frequency problems.
AI.method: FS-PIELM introduces an additive mechanism for weight initialization that translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at unity. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L (independent frequency magnitudes per neuron) and FS-PIELM-G (grouped neurons for robustness). The method preserves ELM computational efficiency via a single linear solve.
AI.result: Experiments on seven benchmark problems (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries show FS-PIELM-L achieves best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants.
AI.conclusion: The proposed additive weight initialization effectively mitigates spectral bias without variance amplification, achieving superior accuracy on high-frequency PDEs while maintaining ELM computational efficiency.

title: DL-VINS-Factory: A Modular Framework for Learned Visual Front-Ends in Visual-Inertial SLAM
summary: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) remains insufficiently characterized. We present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework that integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas--Kanade (LK) optical-flow tracking or LightGlue (LG) descriptor matching. All front-ends share a sliding-window Ceres back-end, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. We benchmark the system across the four datasets covering indoor, unstructured outdoor, aggressive-motion, and visually degraded conditions. Results show that learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM, but are not universally superior to classical tracking. Relative to the corresponding GFTT+LK baseline, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by $5\%$ in monocular odometry and by $7\%$ in stereo with loop-closure. On NTU-VIRAL, where aggressive aerial motion increases inter-frame viewpoint change, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by $12\%$. In Botanic Garden dataset, optical-flow tracking remains preferable, but learned keypoints still improve over the baseline GFTT, in which SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by $29\%$, while RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by $38\%$. On SubT-MRS, learned front-ends display varying degree of improvement based on individual cases. With TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin, all valid configurations run in real time between $29$--$47$ FPS in monocular mode and $18$--$33$ FPS in stereo mode for the EuRoC and NTU-VIRAL datasets. AnyLoc further confirms roughly $2$--$7\times$ more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. The implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/limshoonkit/DL-VINS-Factory-ROS2/.

AI.tldr: DL-VINS-Factory is a unified framework integrating learned visual feature extractors and tracking methods into VI-SLAM, benchmarked across diverse datasets. Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded SLAM but not universally superior to classical methods; they offer specific improvements (e.g., SuperPoint+LK reduces ATE by 29-38% on Botanic Garden) and achieve 29-47 FPS (monocular) / 18-33 FPS (stereo) on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning visual features are well-established for matching tasks, but their practical effectiveness in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) has not been sufficiently characterized or benchmarked.
AI.method: The authors build DL-VINS-Factory, integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with LK optical-flow tracking or LightGlue descriptor matching, all sharing a Ceres sliding-window backend. Optional loop closure uses AnyLoc (DINOv2-VLAD) with 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. TensorRT acceleration runs on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.result: ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by 5% (monocular) and 7% (stereo w/ loop closure). On NTU-VIRAL, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by 12%. On Botanic Garden, SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale ATE by 29%, RaCo+LK reduces RGB ATE by 38%. All valid configurations run at 29-47 FPS (mono) and 18-33 FPS (stereo). AnyLoc finds 2-7× more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2.
AI.conclusion: Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM but not universally superior; their benefits are dataset- and scenario-dependent. The open-source framework enables systematic comparison and adoption in practical systems.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop method for domain-agent post-training that integrates data validation, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide adapter release readiness. On five manufacturing batches, QLoRA-style SFT shows modest gains (overall +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280) but only 3/5 batches improve, GRPO exposes high KL risks, and RAG is necessary for factual extraction.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk, necessitating a systematic closed-loop evaluation framework beyond simple training completion or single offline scores.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records, combining data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to determine adapter suitability.
AI.result: On five manufacturing batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT achieves average gains of +0.0098 overall score, +0.0240 pass rate, +0.0280 evidence accuracy with reduced hallucination/wrong facts. However, only 3/5 batches improve, some regress, GRPO shows high KL risks, and RAG is necessary for factual extraction with increased latency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score, as adapter performance varies across batches and evaluation dimensions.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CROF, a composite validation-time metric combining Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) with structural regularizers from optimal control theory, to predict closed-loop performance of latent world models. Applied to LunarLander v3 with an RSSM world model, CROF selects checkpoints that yield a model-based A2C policy outperforming a model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and also enables strong zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.motivation: Standard validation metrics like loss and multi-step prediction RMSE fail to correlate with downstream closed-loop performance; they keep improving even after control quality collapses. Thus, there is a need for reliable offline diagnostics to select world model checkpoints without requiring expensive online rollouts.
AI.method: The authors train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3, using CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. They evaluate 40 structural diagnostics from optimal control theory, identify Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) as the strongest single predictor, and combine it with three structural regularizers into a composite score called CROF (Composite Reward Observability Fraction).
AI.result: ROF is the best single predictor among 40 metrics. The CROF-selected checkpoint trains a model-based A2C policy that surpasses a model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points with ~65x fewer real-environment steps, and also produces a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop performance of latent world models can be reliably predicted from structural validation-time diagnostics alone, with CROF serving as an effective offline checkpoint selection metric that generalizes across downstream tasks (RL and planning).

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is an inference-time proposal calibration method that improves open-vocabulary object detection by computing a proposal prior combining localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score, achieving +2.5 APr on OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14.
AI.motivation: VLM classification scores lack recognition of object position and scale, leading to false novel activation on background proposals and ranking miscalibration for novel objects.
AI.method: ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining a localization-aware foreground score (capturing whether a proposal contains an object area) and a background-aware suppression score (measuring how much a proposal resembles background).
AI.result: Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-level localization-aware reranking mitigates ranking miscalibration for novel objects, suppressing false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranking true novel proposals above background and partial ones.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: STEER is a gradient-guided attack exploiting safety training gaps in LLMs by translating harmful words into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% attack success rate and transferring to GPT-4o-mini.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs is predominantly in English, leaving generalization to low-resource languages and code-switching unexamined, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently generate harmful responses for out-of-distribution inputs.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement): a gradient-guided attack that identifies words most responsible for refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent.
AI.result: Achieves up to 93.0% attack success rate on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench across six 8B-parameter open-source models; transfers to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% success rate without accessing the target model, outperforming random code-switching and GCG.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs; improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states, deriving a source-centered transport tensor and antisymmetric circulation from observed source-successor pairs. It proves affine covariance, stability, and a separation result showing detection of deterministic recurrent motion beyond infinitesimal geometry, validated on linear-Gaussian models and repeat-copy networks.
AI.motivation: Recurrent representation geometry is typically measured from static snapshots, but recurrent dynamics inherently involve trajectories over time. A framework is needed to capture directed lagged flow and transport from observed state transitions.
AI.method: From observed source-successor pairs (X_t, X_{t+Δ}), estimate a conditional transport law Q_Δ via dense Gaussian source-smoothing. Derive a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ (decomposing into conditional spread and coherent displacement) and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ. Prove affine covariance, estimator stability, and a finite-lag separation result. Validate on linear-Gaussian models and repeat-copy networks.
AI.result: The framework decomposes recurrent dynamics into spread and coherent displacement; circulation summarizes directed lagged flow. It detects deterministic recurrent motion missed by infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry. In repeat-copy networks, reveals architecture-dependent differences in transport scale and coherent displacement trace; coherent displacement fraction is metric- and resolution-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry provides a principled way to analyze recurrent representation dynamics, capturing directed transport and circulation that static geometry misses, with explicit metric dependence and stability guarantees.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic contact maps from text, using contact as an auxiliary modality to improve physical plausibility and reduce artifacts like floating and interpenetration, outperforming prior methods on GRAB and ARCTIC.
AI.motivation: Existing hand-object interaction generation methods suffer from physical plausibility issues like floating and interpenetration due to contact errors, and rely on multi-stage pipelines that fail to model temporally evolving contact dynamics.
AI.method: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic distance-based contact maps from text, treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality to learn contact-motion coupling during training, with contact-guided sampling at inference to enforce consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in both text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Jointly generating contact maps as an auxiliary modality within a single-stage diffusion framework effectively improves temporal stability and reduces physical artifacts in text-driven hand-object interaction generation.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a Neural Architecture Search framework for Camouflaged Object Detection that automatically searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, using a frequency-aware multi-resolution approach with an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture and learnable wavelet transform, achieving state-of-the-art results on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion guided by intuition rather than systematic search, leading to suboptimal performance for detecting camouflaged objects with weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries.
AI.method: CamoNAS employs a frequency-aware multi-resolution NAS framework that automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths in a hierarchical search space. It adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the effectiveness of Neural Architecture Search for Camouflaged Object Detection, demonstrating that automated architecture design outperforms hand-crafted approaches in this domain.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS).
