AI.motivation: Existing binarization methods for LVLMs neglect varying weight importance across different layers and modalities, causing irrelevant parameters to be unnecessarily retained while modality-critical weights are not adequately optimized, leading to significant performance degradation under extreme compression.
AI.method: (1) Construct Hessian matrices for textual and visual inputs; (2) Propose a spatial significance map to distinguish full-precision weights activated under single modality vs. cross-modality; (3) Devise a modality-guided integration strategy to obtain a significance-aware binarization map measuring weight importance across layers and modalities; (4) Incorporate this map as an error reweighting term into the binarization objective; (5) Perform binarization fitting via an alternating significance-weighted update scheme.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate superiority over existing binary PTQ methods under approximately 1-bit compression constraint.
AI.conclusion: The significance-aware binarization approach effectively addresses the modality- and layer-specific weight importance problem in LVLMs, enabling better compression-performance trade-offs for deployment on resource-constrained devices.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes treating memory consolidation in autonomous agents as a deterministic function over episodic memory that produces a separate semantic knowledge layer, rather than altering the agent's core identity. This preserves cryptographic identity invariance while allowing knowledge updates, validated with synthetic experiments showing 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts.
AI.motivation: Long-running adaptive agents face a tension between knowledge consolidation (which conventionally mutates the agent) and the need to maintain cryptographically certified identity for audit and compliance in regulated autonomic deployment.
AI.method: Formalizes consolidation as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory, producing a separately addressable semantic layer that the agent's identity hash does not read. Provides a structural lemma on identity invariance, a deterministic aggregation algorithm with confidence and provenance tracking, and validates with synthetic experiments using Bayesian-shrunk baselines.
AI.result: Demonstrates per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents where lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

title: Many Voices, One Reward: Multi-Role Rubric Generation for LLM Judging and Reward Modeling
summary: Reliable reward and preference signals are critical for evaluating and optimizing large language models on open-ended tasks. Rubric-based judges offer a transparent way to decompose such judgments into explicit evaluation criteria, but existing annotation-free rubric generators typically rely on a single generic evaluator. As a result, they may overlook important dimensions of human preference, a failure mode we term dimensional blind spots. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-Role Rubric Generation (MRRG), a training-free and reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles and consolidates them into an auditable rubric-based scorer. This scorer can be used both to validate pairwise preferences and to provide rewards for GRPO-style Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Experiments on preference validation benchmarks show that MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models. Further RLVR experiments demonstrate that MRRG yields a stronger reward signal for improving open-ended generation.

AI.tldr: MRRG is a training-free framework that generates evaluation rubrics from multiple complementary roles to overcome dimensional blind spots in single-role rubric generators, improving preference validation and reward signals for RLVR.
AI.motivation: Existing annotation-free rubric generators rely on a single generic evaluator, leading to dimensional blind spots where important human preference dimensions are overlooked.
AI.method: Multi-Role Rubric Generation (MRRG): a training-free, reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles and consolidates them into an auditable rubric-based scorer.
AI.result: MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models on preference validation benchmarks, and yields a stronger reward signal for improving open-ended generation in RLVR experiments.
AI.conclusion: Multi-role rubric generation effectively addresses dimensional blind spots in rubric-based judges, providing better preference validation and more reliable rewards for reinforcement learning.

title: Diversity-aware View Partitioning for Scalable VGGT
summary: Geometry transformers such as VGGT achieve strong performance by jointly reasoning over multiple views with global attention. However, scaling them to large view collections remains challenging due to the quadratic cost of attention. Moreover, our empirical analysis reveals that the reconstruction quality in VGGT is sensitive to the distribution of viewpoints. Simply increasing the number of views without sufficient viewpoint diversity can even degrade performance, as redundant views introduce highly similar tokens that dilute informative geometric signals in the attention mechanism. Motivated by this observation, we propose a training-free and plug-and-play VGGT inference framework that organizes views into diversity-aware balanced chunks. The chunks are constructed through combinatorial graph partitioning over visual dissimilarity and spatial dispersion. This view organization allows the transformer to focus attention on geometrically informative views while reducing redundant attention interactions. To estimate spatial dispersion without full pose estimation, we approximate spatial relationships via a soft pose propagation strategy based on visual similarity from a small set of seed frames. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved performance in camera pose estimation, multi-view depth prediction, and 3D reconstruction while reducing memory usage and inference latency. Our framework also complements existing VGGT variants, enabling scalable multi-view reconstruction without sacrificing geometric fidelity.

AI.tldr: A training-free VGGT framework that chunks multi-view inputs into diversity-aware groups via graph partitioning to reduce redundant attention, improving geometric reconstruction quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Scaling geometry transformers (VGGT) to large view collections is challenging due to quadratic attention cost and performance degradation from redundant views with limited viewpoint diversity, which dilute informative geometric signals.
AI.method: Constructs diversity-aware balanced chunks via combinatorial graph partitioning over visual dissimilarity and spatial dispersion; approximates spatial relationships using a soft pose propagation strategy based on visual similarity from seed frames without full pose estimation.
AI.result: Improved camera pose estimation, multi-view depth prediction, and 3D reconstruction while reducing memory usage and inference latency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed plug-and-play framework complements existing VGGT variants, enabling scalable multi-view reconstruction without sacrificing geometric fidelity.

title: Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant
summary: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented multi-agent BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that connects operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation to improve O&M decision-making.
AI.motivation: Large-scale BESSs face complex O&M decisions combining multiple data sources (alarms, cell measurements, topology, diagnostics, maintenance docs), but existing monitoring platforms only flag threshold violations without explaining root causes (e.g., voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, thermal abnormality).
AI.method: A traceable fault-diagnosis assistant using retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning, featuring BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained NL database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis.
AI.result: Preliminary internal evaluation reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning components.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent system improves reliability by connecting operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation in a traceable manner for BESS fault diagnosis.

title: Adaptive Group-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Time-Series Rehabilitation Data
comment: To be published at IEEE CBMS 2026
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) for multivariate time-series classifiers are often difficult to interpret in domains where experts reason in terms of semantic feature groups rather than individual channels. In rehabilitation movement analysis with multi-sensor inertial measurement units (IMUs), clinicians interpret motion through muscle-group and joint-segment abstractions; yet, most existing counterfactual methods operate at the channel level, producing scattered and biomechanically incoherent explanations. We propose a two-stage framework for group-based counterfactual generation in high-dimensional IMU data. We first show that Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking preserves counterfactual validity but fails to enforce group-level sparsity, motivating the need for explicit group selection. We then introduce Learnable Gate (LG) methods, which incorporate trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks. Experiments on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset demonstrate that LG substantially improves modality-group sparsity compared to the channel-level M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses further show that group-structured counterfactuals yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning. Overall, the proposed framework enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis.

AI.tldr: Proposes a two-stage framework (Shapley-Adaptive ranking + Learnable Gates) for generating group-based counterfactual explanations for multivariate time-series IMU data in rehabilitation, achieving better sparsity and interpretability than channel-level methods while maintaining validity and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanations for multivariate time-series operate at the channel level, producing scattered and biomechanically incoherent explanations that are difficult for clinicians who reason in terms of semantic feature groups (e.g., muscle groups, joint segments).
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking for ordering, and (2) Learnable Gate (LG) methods with trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks to enforce group-level sparsity.
AI.result: LG substantially improves modality-group sparsity compared to M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset. Exercise-specific analyses show group-structured counterfactuals yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis.

title: FoundDP: Revisiting Weak Disparity Observability in Dual-Pixel Depth Estimation
summary: Dual-pixel (DP) imaging enables metric depth estimation from a single camera using sub-aperture disparity. However, the extremely small effective baseline limits disparity observability, leading to structural degradation and depth failure in textureless, low-contrast, or downsampled regions. Existing DP-based methods rely primarily on local disparity cues and therefore become unreliable when disparity signals are weak or ambiguous. To address this limitation, we propose \emph{FoundDP}, a unified framework that integrates metric DP depth with global structural priors from a monocular depth foundation model. Our method preserves metric scale through DP-derived depth and leverages Vision Transformer (ViT) features to restore structural consistency in weak-disparity regions. To ensure reliable metric guidance under DP imaging conditions, we identify and mitigate ViT representation degradation induced by DP defocus blur via ViT feature alignment, enabling stable metric-guided depth estimation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world DP benchmarks show that FoundDP delivers superior performance, with consistent gains in structural fidelity and metric accuracy, especially under reduced disparity observability. Code will be available at: https://github.com/EchoLighting/FoundDP

AI.tldr: FoundDP integrates dual-pixel (DP) disparity with monocular depth foundation model priors to achieve robust metric depth estimation, especially in weak-disparity regions. It addresses DP defocus blur via ViT feature alignment, demonstrating superior structural fidelity and metric accuracy on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Dual-pixel imaging suffers from limited disparity observability in textureless, low-contrast, or downsampled regions, and existing DP-based methods relying on local disparity cues become unreliable when signals are weak or ambiguous.
AI.method: Proposes FoundDP, a unified framework that combines DP-derived metric depth with global structural priors from a monocular depth foundation model using ViT features. It mitigates DP defocus blur degradation via ViT feature alignment to ensure stable metric guidance.
AI.result: Superior performance on synthetic and real-world DP benchmarks, with consistent gains in structural fidelity and metric accuracy, particularly under reduced disparity observability.
AI.conclusion: FoundDP effectively resolves the structural degradation and depth failure in weak-disparity DP imaging regions by fusing local metric DP depth with global monocular priors and addressing defocus blur degradation through feature alignment.

title: InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories
summary: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

AI.tldr: InduceKV is a retrieval-based method for fixed-footprint continual adaptation of multimodal LLMs, storing compact KV-payload memory entries selected via bilevel optimization to balance likelihood, retention, and coverage under strict memory budgets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs need to continually adapt to evolving tasks/domains, but repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores accumulate adaptation state over time, making continual improvement difficult under bounded deployment footprints.
AI.method: InduceKV stores selected training prefixes as attention-ready memory entries (frozen retrieval key + compact layerwise KV payloads) appended to self-attention cache. A bilevel selection constructs a compact inducing set: lightweight calibration fits retrieval, while selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in frozen retrieval space under strict memory budget.
AI.result: Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently outperforms PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. Gains are not due to stronger backbone, replay alone, or unbounded candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: InduceKV provides an effective fixed-footprint continual adaptation paradigm by externalizing task-specific updates as compact retrieval-based memory entries, avoiding parameter updates or growing replay stores while maintaining strong performance across diverse continual learning scenarios.

title: Rethinking Post-Hoc Calibration in Semantic Segmentation
summary: Reliable confidence estimates are essential in semantic segmentation, especially in safety-critical settings where overconfident errors can mislead downstream decisions. Yet modern segmentation models often remain miscalibrated. Post-hoc calibration offers a practical way to correct confidence estimates without retraining the segmentation model, but its use in dense prediction raises structural issues that are often overlooked. We study two such issues. First, adding a constant to all logits leaves the softmax probabilities unchanged, but several standard calibrators can still depend on this arbitrary offset. As a result, two logit representations encoding the same predictive distribution may yield different calibrated probabilities. We define translation-invariant (TI) calibrators as those whose outputs are unchanged under such shifts, characterize which common calibrators satisfy this property, and construct TI counterparts of shift-sensitive calibrators to isolate the effect of removing representation dependence. Second, post-hoc calibration is typically fitted by minimizing a likelihood-based objective, whereas segmentation models are trained with task-specific metrics such as Dice. This mismatch can cause calibration to alter class orderings and degrade the deployed segmentation map. We study decision-preserving calibration under argmax- and order-preservation constraints. Since enforcing these constraints collapses affine softmax calibrators to temperature scaling, we introduce class-conditional affine calibrators that can be made argmax- or order-preserving while retaining greater expressivity, allowing us to quantify the calibration-segmentation trade-off induced by decision preservation. Across natural-image and medical segmentation benchmarks, and under corruption-based covariate shift, matched comparisons show that TI variants generally improve calibration metrics, while decision-preserving variants prevent segmentation degradation and retain strong calibration performance. These results provide practical design principles for well-defined post-hoc calibration pipelines in semantic segmentation.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and addresses two structural issues in post-hoc calibration for semantic segmentation: (1) translation invariance, where standard calibrators can depend on arbitrary logit offsets that do not affect softmax probabilities, and (2) decision preservation, where likelihood-based calibration objectives conflict with task-specific segmentation metrics (e.g., Dice), potentially degrading segmentation maps. The authors propose translation-invariant (TI) variants of shift-sensitive calibrators and decision-preserving (argmax/order-preserving) versions of class-conditional affine calibrators. Experiments on natural-image and medical segmentation benchmarks show TI variants improve calibration metrics while decision-preserving variants prevent segmentation degradation without sacrificing calibration performance.
AI.motivation: Reliable confidence estimates are critical in safety-critical semantic segmentation applications where overconfident errors can mislead downstream decisions. Modern segmentation models are often miscalibrated, and while post-hoc calibration is a practical solution, its application to dense prediction tasks introduces structural issues (translation invariance and decision preservation) that have been overlooked in prior work.
AI.method: The authors formally define translation-invariant (TI) calibrators, characterize which common calibrators satisfy TI, and construct TI counterparts of shift-sensitive calibrators. They also study decision-preserving calibration under argmax- and order-preservation constraints, showing that enforcing these constraints collapses affine softmax calibrators to temperature scaling, then introduce class-conditional affine calibrators that can be made argmax- or order-preserving while retaining expressivity.
AI.result: Across natural-image and medical segmentation benchmarks under corruption-based covariate shift, TI variants generally improve calibration metrics compared to their shift-sensitive counterparts. Decision-preserving variants prevent segmentation degradation while retaining strong calibration performance, effectively managing the calibration-segmentation trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The results provide practical design principles for well-defined post-hoc calibration pipelines in semantic segmentation, highlighting the importance of addressing translation invariance and decision preservation to ensure both reliable confidence estimates and preserved segmentation quality.

title: Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails
summary: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost. Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies hidden evidence-use forgetting in continually adapted multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), where answer accuracy stays correct but the model silently shifts its grounding evidence. It proposes RCL, a replay-free framework that freezes previous checkpoints, estimates evidence-reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation. RCL outperforms baselines across multiple benchmarks in reducing modality reliance drift and hidden forgetting.
AI.motivation: Standard continual learning metrics only check if answers remain correct, ignoring whether the model's underlying multimodal evidence grounding (visual, textual, OCR, chart, document) remains stable. This leaves a critical failure mode—hidden evidence-use forgetting—unexamined and unaddressed.
AI.method: RCL (Reliance-Constrained Continual Learning): freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions (ablating individual modality channels), and jointly optimizes three objectives—task learning, prediction preservation (output logit consistency), and reliance preservation (evidence channel usage consistency)—without requiring replay or adding inference cost.
AI.result: Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, RCL consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates.
AI.conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves. RCL demonstrates that explicitly constraining evidence-reliance stability is both feasible and necessary for trustworthy continual adaptation of MLLMs.

title: Learning the Supports for Categorical Critic in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Value functions are an essential component in actor-critic based deep reinforcement learning (RL). Conventionally, these functions are trained as a regression task by minimising the mean squared error (MSE) relative to bootstrapped target values. Meanwhile, in distributional RL, a distribution of returns is modelled based on the distributional Bellman operator. This work investigates the Gaussian Histogram Loss (HL-Gauss), a recent approach that reframes value estimation as classification by encoding each scalar Bellman target as a Gaussian-smoothed categorical target. Despite its potential, applying histogram-based losses to RL presents inherent challenges, most notably the requirement to pre-define a fixed support interval, which is often complicated by the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values typically found in RL tasks. In this work, we propose an approach that dynamically learns the lower and upper bounds of the support instead of assigning them beforehand. We derive an objective that jointly learns these bounds whilst learning the categorical representation of the scalar values, and we show that this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error. Our theoretical analysis further shows that this bound is tighter than that of non-learned supports of HL-Gauss. Empirically, the proposed objective enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks whilst improving on a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes dynamically learning the support bounds for histogram-based value estimation in distributional RL, instead of pre-specifying them, and shows this forms a tighter upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error while achieving competitive or better performance on continuous-control tasks.
AI.motivation: Histogram-based losses (HL-Gauss) require pre-defining a fixed support interval for value estimation, which is problematic due to the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values in RL. The authors aim to remove this manual specification by learning the support bounds dynamically.
AI.method: The authors derive an objective that jointly learns the lower and upper bounds of the categorical support alongside the categorical representation of scalar values. They theoretically analyze this objective as an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error and show it is tighter than HL-Gauss with non-learned supports.
AI.result: The proposed approach enables stable adaptation of the support interval, matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks, and improves on a subset, all without requiring a pre-specified support interval.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically learning the support bounds for histogram-based value estimation is a viable and theoretically grounded alternative to pre-specified intervals, removing a key limitation of HL-Gauss while maintaining or improving performance in continuous-control RL tasks.

title: SFKD: Spatial--Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation via Multi-Level Wavelet Spectral Interaction
summary: Most existing knowledge distillation methods focus on homogeneous models (e.g., CNN-to-CNN), thereby overlooking the flexibility and potential of knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models. Due to intrinsic inductive bias discrepancies between heterogeneous models that cause spatial distribution inconsistencies, prior heterogeneous distillation methods often weaken or discard spatial information in heterogeneous representations. However, the spatial information in representations often encodes transferable global structural semantics as well as architecture-specific local details, and therefore should not be directly ignored. To better leverage the spatial information encoded in heterogeneous representations, we propose a Spatial-Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation framework (SFKD). By leveraging the complementary properties of wavelet transform spatial locality and Fourier representations in characterizing global energy distributions, we first apply multi-level discrete wavelet transform to explicitly decouple spatial information. The resulting wavelet sub-bands are further refined by a dual-stream dual-stage refinement module, and finally combined with a Gaussian-filtered frequency loss to selectively capture informative global information. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under both homogeneous and heterogeneous models demonstrate the superiority of our method.

AI.tldr: Proposes SFKD, a heterogeneous knowledge distillation framework that uses wavelet transforms and Fourier representations to preserve and leverage spatial information from heterogeneous model representations, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous knowledge distillation methods often weaken or discard spatial information in heterogeneous representations due to spatial distribution inconsistencies caused by inductive bias discrepancies between different model architectures, but spatial information encodes transferable global structural semantics and architecture-specific local details that should not be ignored.
AI.method: Proposes Spatial-Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation (SFKD) which: (1) applies multi-level discrete wavelet transform to decouple spatial information, leveraging complementary properties of wavelet spatial locality and Fourier global energy distributions; (2) refines wavelet sub-bands via a dual-stream dual-stage refinement module; (3) combines with Gaussian-filtered frequency loss to selectively capture informative global information.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under both homogeneous and heterogeneous models demonstrate the superiority of SFKD over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Spatial information in heterogeneous representations should be preserved and leveraged for knowledge distillation, and the joint spatial-frequency approach via wavelet and Fourier transforms effectively achieves this cross-architecture knowledge transfer.

title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PACE predicts LLM agent performance on expensive agentic benchmarks (e.g., SWE-Bench, GAIA) using scores from a small, carefully selected subset of cheap non-agentic evaluation instances, achieving under 4% MAE, >0.80 Spearman correlation, and ~85% ranking accuracy at <1% of full agentic evaluation cost.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA is prohibitively expensive (thousands of dollars, days to complete) and requires complex infrastructure, while non-agentic benchmarks are fast and cheap. The authors aim to predict agentic performance accurately without the overhead of full agent evaluation.
AI.method: PACE constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting atomic instances from existing non-agentic evaluations using two complementary strategies: target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. A regression model maps scores on the selected source instances to target agentic benchmark scores.
AI.result: Across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV MAE under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, pairwise model-ranking accuracy ~85%, at less than 1% of full agentic evaluation cost.
AI.conclusion: PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing without the overhead of full agent evaluation, and the analysis reveals which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands.

title: Regularized Variational and Spectral Log-Density-Ratio Estimation in the Gaussian Location Model
summary: We study ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in the Gaussian location model with a common covariance matrix. By affine invariance, the model is written as q $\sim$ N(0, I), p $\sim$ N($Δ$, I), with linear features, where $Δ$ is a mean vector. The variational estimator is the empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) log-normalized fit with a squared L2-penalty on its nonconstant coefficient, and the spectral estimator recently introduced in [1] replaces a single variational problem by a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. We derive high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents when the numbers of observations and dimension tend to infinity with fixed ratios. The regularized variational limit is characterized by a scalar entropy minimization problem derived from the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT), while the regularized spectral limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. We use these formulas to compare population risks, with experiments focused on fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. Our conclusion is that with many observations, under the criteria and asymptotic regimes analyzed here, the well-specified variational estimator has the smaller risk, while with fewer observations, the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction has lower variance. We also study how a nuclear penalty can be used and partially analyzed to perform feature learning.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in a Gaussian location model, deriving asymptotic equivalents for variational and spectral estimators, and comparing their risks under different observation regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand and compare the performance of variational and spectral estimators for regularized log-density-ratio estimation in high-dimensional settings, particularly under different observation-to-dimension ratios.
AI.method: The paper uses the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT) to characterize the regularized variational limit via scalar entropy minimization, and deterministic equivalents for resolvents to derive spectral limits. It assumes proportional asymptotics where observations and dimensions grow with fixed ratio.
AI.result: With many observations, the well-specified variational estimator has smaller risk; with fewer observations, the spectral estimator has lower variance and is favored. A nuclear penalty is also studied for feature learning.
AI.conclusion: The choice between variational and spectral estimators depends on the observation regime: variational is better for large-sample settings, spectral for small-sample settings due to its covariance-based construction reducing variance.

title: Towards Real-World Ultrasound Understanding: Large Vision-Language Models from Multi-Image Examinations with Long-Form Reports
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have achieved strong performance across many medical imaging tasks, yet their application to ultrasound remains limited due to its inherent complexity and variability. In this work, we revisit what is truly needed to enable real-world ultrasound understanding. Instead of introducing complex architectures or elaborate training strategies, we show that data scale and clinically faithful data alignment are the key factors. We construct a large-scale dataset of 1.5M real-world ultrasound examinations, containing 17.7M images, multi-organ coverage, and paired uncurated clinical reports. Crucially, we organize the data at the examination level, aligning multiple images with their corresponding reports to reflect real clinical workflows. We then fine-tune a standard LVLM using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on this dataset without task-specific modifications. Surprisingly, this simple recipe already leads to strong performance across diverse ultrasound understanding tasks, outperforming prior methods designed with more complex pipelines. Beyond these results, we present model and data scaling analyses that provide insights into the role of scale in ultrasound LVLMs.

AI.tldr: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA on a large-scale dataset of 1.5M ultrasound exams (17.7M images) with examination-level clinical report alignment achieve strong performance across diverse ultrasound tasks, outperforming more complex prior methods, with scaling analyses revealing the critical role of data scale and clinically faithful alignment.
AI.motivation: LVLMs have shown promise in medical imaging but remain limited in ultrasound due to its inherent complexity and variability. Prior approaches rely on complex architectures or elaborate training strategies. The authors aim to demonstrate that data scale and clinically faithful data alignment — not architectural complexity — are the key enablers for real-world ultrasound understanding.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale dataset of 1.5M real-world ultrasound examinations containing 17.7M images with multi-organ coverage and paired uncurated clinical reports, organized at the examination level (multiple images aligned with corresponding reports). They fine-tune a standard LVLM using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on this dataset without any task-specific modifications.
AI.result: The simple fine-tuning recipe outperforms prior methods with more complex pipelines across diverse ultrasound understanding tasks. The authors also present model and data scaling analyses providing insights into the role of scale in ultrasound LVLMs.
AI.conclusion: Data scale and clinically faithful examination-level alignment are the primary drivers for effective ultrasound understanding in LVLMs, rather than complex architectures or training strategies. Scaling analyses further underscore the importance of dataset size and realistic clinical data organization.

title: Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees
comment: Proc. Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML-PKDD 2026), LNCS, Naples, Italy, 7-11 September 2026
summary: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC), a formal framework for exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees using semiring-based computation, achieving polynomial-time complexity in the number of features for tasks like optimization, counting, and sampling, with demonstrated utility on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space, but the doubly exponential hypothesis space of decision trees makes exhaustive analysis challenging.
AI.method: ADTC reformulates analytical tasks (optimization, counting, sampling) into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring R, inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC). A dynamic programming algorithm achieves O*(n^{O(Δ)}) time complexity. Model behavior tensors aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring to handle complex multi-metric constraints.
AI.result: The dynamic programming algorithm achieves O*(n^{O(Δ)}) time complexity (n = number of features, Δ = max depth), down from doubly exponential. The framework efficiently constructs model profiles capturing global landscape and trade-offs between accuracy, size, and fairness. Software toolkit emtrees demonstrated on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains by providing a global view of the hypothesis space and enabling systematic trade-off analysis across multiple criteria.

title: Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress
summary: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

AI.tldr: Rank-Then-Act (RTA) learns control policies from expert video demonstrations by training a VLM as a progress-based ordinal scorer via GRPO on shuffled frames, then using Spearman rank correlation as a reward signal for RL, achieving strong results across discrete and continuous control tasks without explicit rewards.
AI.motivation: To learn control policies from expert video demonstrations without requiring environment rewards, overcoming the need for explicit reward engineering by leveraging ordinal supervision from video sequences.
AI.method: (1) Train a VLM offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer using GRPO over shuffled frame sequences. (2) Use Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices as a bounded, scale-invariant reward function for RL. (3) Decouple reward learning from absolute calibration.
AI.result: RTA matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines on PyBoy (Catrap, Kirby), PointMaze, and MetaWorld, with strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer.
AI.conclusion: Correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

title: Robust Image Processing Techniques for Construction Environment Monitoring Using Underwater Robots
summary: This paper proposes a robust image processing framework for underwater robot-based construction environment monitoring, targeting complex degradations observed in real marine environments. Unlike conventional approaches that mainly consider absorption and backscattering, real underwater imagery is strongly affected by depth-dependent forward scattering blur and particle-induced degradations such as marine snow. To address this, we introduce a staged processing pipeline that sequentially models background degradation via depth-aware forward scattering and foreground degradation using realistic marine snow patterns extracted from real images. The resulting synthetic data are used to retrain an existing Joint-ID network without modifying its architecture, enabling an isolated evaluation of dataset realism. In addition, a lightweight post-processing scheme is applied to enhance contrast and structural clarity. Experiments on real underwater datasets collected in Korean coastal environments demonstrate consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores. The results indicate that explicitly modeling forward scattering and realistic particle effects effectively reduces the synthetic-to-real gap and improves practical applicability in real-world underwater robotic operations.

AI.tldr: A robust image processing framework for underwater robot monitoring that models depth-dependent forward scattering and marine snow effects to retrain a Joint-ID network, improving visual quality and reducing synthetic-to-real gap in real marine environments.
AI.motivation: Conventional underwater image enhancement approaches mainly consider absorption and backscattering, neglecting depth-dependent forward scattering blur and particle-induced degradations like marine snow, which are prevalent in real marine environments and cause a significant synthetic-to-real gap.
AI.method: A staged processing pipeline with (1) depth-aware forward scattering modeling for background degradation, (2) realistic marine snow patterns extracted from real images for foreground degradation, (3) retraining an existing Joint-ID network on synthetic data without architecture modification, and (4) a lightweight post-processing scheme for contrast and structural clarity enhancement.
AI.result: Experiments on real underwater datasets from Korean coastal environments show consistent improvements in visual quality and UIQM scores, demonstrating that explicit modeling of forward scattering and realistic particle effects effectively reduces the synthetic-to-real gap.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling forward scattering and realistic particle effects reduces the synthetic-to-real gap and improves practical applicability in real-world underwater robotic operations.

title: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

AI.tldr: Maven is a reinforcement learning framework with editable evidence memory that rewards intermediate actions (add, link, drop) based on state transitions, outperforming outcome-only RL on long-context reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context RL methods reward only final answers or static evidence extraction, lacking feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state during reasoning.
AI.method: Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and provides action-level rewards: add actions get marginal gain and hindsight contribution credits, link actions get evidence synergy rewards, and drop actions get improved answer support rewards. These rewards are assigned to corresponding action spans in GRPO.
AI.result: Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention.
AI.conclusion: Long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

title: Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization for Bandwidth-Efficient Collaborative 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction
summary: Collaborative perception extends single-agent perception by enabling multiple vehicles to exchange complementary perceptual information. However, it introduces an inherent trade-off between perception gain and communication overhead, which is particularly severe for 3D semantic occupancy prediction that relies on fine-grained spatial structures. Existing methods typically compress 3D features into 2D, causing severe spatial information loss, or transmit dense 3D representations, hindering real-world deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose a bandwidth-efficient collaborative Vector Quantization Semantic Occupancy Prediction (VQSOP) framework. VQSOP employs a Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization (SAVQ) mechanism that exploits 3D scene sparsity to compactly encode informative regions, drastically reducing communication overhead while preserving complete geometric context. Furthermore, to enhance structural consistency and feature continuity, we design a Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement (ASR) module that dynamically fuses local high-frequency details with broad contextual semantics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing communication volume by up to 82x.

AI.tldr: VQSOP is a bandwidth-efficient collaborative perception framework for 3D semantic occupancy prediction that uses Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization (SAVQ) to exploit 3D scene sparsity for compact encoding and a Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement (ASR) module for structural consistency, achieving SOTA performance with up to 82x communication reduction.
AI.motivation: Collaborative perception for 3D semantic occupancy prediction faces a critical trade-off between perception gain and communication overhead. Existing methods either compress 3D features into 2D (causing severe spatial information loss) or transmit dense 3D representations (hindering real-world deployment), motivating the need for a bandwidth-efficient solution that preserves geometric context.
AI.method: The VQSOP framework consists of two key components: (1) Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization (SAVQ) mechanism that exploits 3D scene sparsity to compactly encode informative regions, reducing communication overhead while preserving complete geometric context; (2) Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement (ASR) module that dynamically fuses local high-frequency details with broad contextual semantics to enhance structural consistency and feature continuity.
AI.result: The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing communication volume by up to 82x.
AI.conclusion: VQSOP effectively overcomes the limitations of prior collaborative perception methods for 3D semantic occupancy prediction by leveraging scene sparsity and adaptive feature refinement, enabling bandwidth-efficient deployment without sacrificing perceptual quality.

title: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
summary: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA uses prediction-error-driven (surprise-based) chunking with a decoupled training strategy and internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to achieve accurate long-horizon predictions (250+ timesteps) where baselines fail within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) suffer from misaligned chunk boundaries when using fixed-length or similarity-based methods. The paper argues that chunking should be driven by prediction errors (surprise), as these directly indicate when longer-range context is needed.
AI.method: Proposes Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA) with: (1) a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and prevent hierarchical collapse, and (2) internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries during imagined rollouts (open-loop prediction).
AI.result: On video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments, SUNTA outperforms baselines and uniquely maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, while all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Surprise-based chunking with decoupled training and internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric effectively enables long-horizon predictions in hierarchical state-space models by aligning chunk boundaries with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data.

title: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
comment: The 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a population-based multi-objective evolutionary training strategy for SSL-GANs, where discriminators are ranked by Pareto dominance to balance classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, improving training robustness and classification accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: SSL-GANs can leverage unlabeled data but suffer from training instability due to the conflicting objectives of classification and real/fake discrimination being aggregated into a single scalar loss.
AI.method: Formulates discriminator learning as a multi-objective optimization problem using population-based evolutionary training with Pareto dominance ranking, maintaining a diverse set of discriminators that explore different trade-offs between supervised and unsupervised objectives. Variants include an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation.
AI.result: On MNIST with limited labels, the proposed method shows improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN, with the elitist variant achieving the highest classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization effectively stabilizes SSL-GAN training and improves both classifier accuracy and generator quality, with the elitist strategy being the most effective variant.

title: LiZAD: A Lightweight Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection Framework for Industrial Manufacturing
comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Omni-Layer Intelligent Systems (COINS) 2026
summary: In modern high-throughput industrial production lines, product configurations and visual characteristics frequently change, making it impractical to collect and annotate data for every new scenario. This dynamic setting makes Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection (ZSAD) particularly suitable, as it enables defect detection without requiring training on target-specific samples. Although recent ZSAD approaches show promising results, they are computationally intensive and thus unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. We propose LiZAD: a lightweight framework designed for real-time ZSAD specifically tailored for use on edge devices. The proposed approach pairs the dense and spatially aware visual features of DINOv3, crucial for precise pixel-level localization, with the highly computationally efficient text embeddings of MobileCLIP2. These features are then mapped into a shared latent space via low-memory trainable projection heads. Compared to six state-of-the-art ZSAD models, LiZAD achieves an average memory reduction of 61.5%, a parameter reduction of 74.6%, and a speedup of 3.02x in terms of latency. Despite substantial reductions in computational and memory costs, our approach maintains competitive anomaly detection performance, dropping the average P-AUROC by just 6.4% relative to the best state-of-the-art model across the VisA, BTAD, MPDD, and MVTec-AD datasets. Finally, it is successfully deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson NX and Jetson AGX edge devices and tested on the real production line of the Industrial Computer Engineering Laboratory (ICE Lab) at the University of Verona. The code is available at https://github.com/intelligolabs/LiZAD.

AI.tldr: LiZAD is a lightweight zero-shot anomaly detection framework optimized for edge devices, combining DINOv3 visual features with MobileCLIP2 text embeddings via trainable projection heads, achieving 61.5% memory reduction, 74.6% parameter reduction, and 3.02x speedup while maintaining competitive performance, deployed on NVIDIA Jetson edge devices and tested on a real production line.
AI.motivation: Existing ZSAD methods are computationally intensive and unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices, while modern production lines face frequently changing product configurations where data collection and annotation for each new scenario is impractical.
AI.method: LiZAD pairs DINOv3's dense spatial visual features with MobileCLIP2's efficient text embeddings, mapping them into a shared latent space via low-memory trainable projection heads.
AI.result: Achieves 61.5% memory reduction, 74.6% parameter reduction, 3.02x speedup versus six SOTA ZSAD models; drops average P-AUROC by only 6.4% relative to best SOTA; successfully deployed on NVIDIA Jetson NX and AGX edge devices and tested on a real production line.
AI.conclusion: LiZAD demonstrates that lightweight zero-shot anomaly detection on edge devices is feasible with competitive performance, enabling real-time deployment in dynamic industrial settings.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults that provides context governance (provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction) as a layer beneath retrieval. Experiments show it Pareto-dominates BM25 in stale-version attacks (97% vs 90-93% pass rate at 1/3 token cost) and achieves deterministic retrieval (Jaccard 1.0) where dense+HNSW fails (mean Jaccard 0.611).
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents depend on external knowledge stores but existing retrieval pipelines only provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. The paper formalizes this gap as "context governance" and aims to address failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve.
AI.method: ContextNext combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, MCP source nodes for live data, and audit traces of agent context consumption. It operates as a governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
AI.result: In a stale-version attack, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over 1,060 documents, ContextNext and BM25 achieve Jaccard 1.0 (deterministic), while dense+HNSW is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).
AI.conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. The results suggest that governed selection provides better answer quality, lower cost, and deterministic behavior compared to ungoverned retrieval approaches. The core engine, CLI, and MCP server are released under open licenses.

title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis
summary: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

AI.tldr: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model that uses a multi-scale Transformer with point-wise tokenization and U-shaped hierarchy, plus Multi-Objective Temporal Masking, to achieve competitive performance across multiple time series tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Previous TSFMs focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other analysis tasks. Zeus aims to bridge this gap by achieving multi-task generalization without tuning.
AI.method: (1) Multi-scale Transformer with point-wise tokenization and U-shaped hierarchy to balance fine-grained fidelity and computational efficiency. (2) Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM) as a unified pre-training strategy supporting heterogeneous tasks like extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction.
AI.result: Zeus achieves competitive results across five representative tasks in tuning-free settings, demonstrating superior multi-task generalization.
AI.conclusion: Zeus demonstrates strong potential as a general-purpose TSFM, enabling competitive performance across diverse time series tasks without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Personalized 4D Whole-Heart Mesh Reconstruction from Cine MRI via Multi-Scale Temporal Modeling and Differentiable Contour Rendering
summary: Accurate 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI is critical for creating cardiac digital twins, but remains challenging due to limited 2D slice coverage and the complex coupling between cardiac shape and motion. Existing methods often rely on intermediate contour fitting and typically reconstruct static, single-phase, or partial cardiac geometries, limiting their ability to capture full-chamber dynamics. We propose a novel end-to-end framework for reconstructing temporally resolved whole-heart meshes from multi-view 2D cine MRI sequences by learning an image-to-mesh mapping. The framework incorporates a differentiable contour renderer inspired by the Beer-Lambert attenuation principle, enabling anatomy-aware supervision of 3D+t mesh deformation through contour-based projection losses. To improve temporal consistency across the cardiac cycle, we further introduce a multi-scale temporal modeling module that integrates global cycle-level dynamics with local inter-frame coherence to generate smooth and physiologically plausible mesh trajectories. The proposed method achieved a whole-heart mean absolute error of 1.68 $\pm$ 0.31 mm and a motion jitter of 0.77 $\pm$ 0.17 $\mathrm{mm}/\mathrm{frame}^{3}$, outperforming existing methods with lower reconstruction error and substantially improved motion smoothness. It also improved 2D contour alignment across multiple cine MRI views and supported downstream proof-of-concept electrophysiological simulation. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

AI.tldr: A novel end-to-end framework for reconstructing temporally resolved 4D whole-heart meshes from sparse multi-view 2D cine MRI by learning image-to-mesh mapping, using a differentiable contour renderer with Beer-Lambert-based supervision and a multi-scale temporal modeling module, achieving superior accuracy (1.68 mm MAE) and motion smoothness (0.77 mm/frame³ jitter).
AI.motivation: Accurate 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI is critical for creating cardiac digital twins, but remains challenging due to limited 2D slice coverage and complex coupling between cardiac shape and motion. Existing methods rely on intermediate contour fitting and typically reconstruct static, single-phase, or partial cardiac geometries, limiting their ability to capture full-chamber dynamics.
AI.method: An end-to-end framework with (1) an image-to-mesh mapping that directly reconstructs 3D+t meshes from multi-view 2D cine MRI; (2) a differentiable contour renderer based on Beer-Lambert attenuation for anatomy-aware supervision via contour projection losses; and (3) a multi-scale temporal modeling module combining global cycle-level dynamics with local inter-frame coherence for smooth, physiologically plausible mesh trajectories.
AI.result: Whole-heart MAE of 1.68 ± 0.31 mm and motion jitter of 0.77 ± 0.17 mm/frame³, outperforming existing methods with lower reconstruction error and substantially improved motion smoothness, plus improved 2D contour alignment across multiple cine MRI views and successful downstream electrophysiological simulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end framework effectively addresses the challenges of 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and motion smoothness, enabling downstream cardiac digital twin applications such as electrophysiological simulation.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne is a series of fitness-specialized LLMs (8B/32B) built on Qwen3, using a three-stage post-training pipeline (continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning) that achieves significant improvements on professional fitness exams (ACSM-EP, NSCA-CSCS) by up to 12.73% while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) by human professionals is costly and inaccessible; general-purpose LLMs lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios.
