Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

AI.tldr: SA-HGNN is a hyperbolic graph neural network that dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies, uses hyperbolic graph convolution to capture hierarchical structures, and employs attention pooling to filter noise, achieving superior depression recognition from EEG data.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based methods for EEG depression recognition capture spatial functional connectivity but fail to accurately model the inherent hierarchical structure of brain networks in depressed patients, leading to suboptimal connectivity pattern extraction.
AI.method: SA-HGNN consists of three modules: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction for dynamically building personalized brain network topologies; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution to capture latent hierarchical relationships beyond Euclidean representation limits; (3) Attention Pooling to adaptively filter high-redundancy noise channels.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate superior performance across both resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating robustness to noise and effectiveness in capturing abnormal functional connectivity in depressed patients' brain networks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SA-HGNN effectively addresses the hierarchical structure challenge in depression brain networks by combining sample-adaptive graph construction, hyperbolic geometry, and attention-based noise filtering, outperforming existing methods.

title: Evaluating Vision-Language Models as a Zero-Shot Learning Alternative to You Only Look Once and Optical Character Recognition for Nigerian License Plate Recognition
summary: License Plate Recognition (LPR) systems are critical tools in traffic monitoring, security enforcement, and urban mobility management. Traditional LPR systems often rely on a multi-stage pipeline involving object detection using You Only Look Once (YOLO) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), which suffer from limitations such as high resource demands, poor performance in unstructured environments, and the need for large annotated datasets. This study explores the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a unified, zeroshot learning solution for Nigerian license plate recognition. Using a curated dataset of 88 challenging real-world images collected in Nigeria, we evaluate five selected VLMs: Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp (Google DeepMind), Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Alibaba), GPT-4o (OpenAI), Claude 4 Sonnet (Anthropic), and Llama 3.2 Vision 90b (Meta). Results based on Character Error Rate (CER) reveal that Gemini and Qwen significantly outperform other models in both accuracy and robustness, on the challenging image scenarios. This work highlights the practical advantages of VLMs over YOLO+OCR, questions the claims by model providers, and compares the performances of the VLMs.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates five Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Nigerian license plate recognition as a unified zero-shot alternative to traditional YOLO+OCR pipelines. Using a dataset of 88 challenging real-world images, Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct significantly outperform GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Llama 3.2 Vision 90b in terms of Character Error Rate (CER), demonstrating VLMs' practical advantages over multi-stage approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional LPR systems using YOLO+OCR pipelines suffer from high resource demands, poor performance in unstructured environments, and reliance on large annotated datasets. This work explores VLMs as a unified zero-shot solution to overcome these limitations, specifically for Nigerian license plates in challenging real-world conditions.
AI.method: Five VLMs (Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, Llama 3.2 Vision 90b) were evaluated on a curated dataset of 88 challenging real-world Nigerian license plate images using Character Error Rate (CER) as the evaluation metric.
AI.result: Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct significantly outperformed the other three models in both accuracy and robustness across challenging image scenarios based on CER.
AI.conclusion: VLMs demonstrate practical advantages over traditional YOLO+OCR pipelines for LPR. The work also questions claims made by model providers and provides performance comparisons across VLMs.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

AI.tldr: We present a pipeline for autonomous research agents in frontier physical science that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 condensed-matter physics papers to a publication-grade manuscript on altermagnetic piezomagnetism, using literature-anchored calibration via 2,162 consultation events across 47 sessions, with fault tolerance from redundancy and bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures.
AI.motivation: Frontier physical science differs from ML sandboxes: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors rather than execution feedback, which unscaffolded agents fail to do properly.
AI.method: A six-phase pipeline (47 fresh-context sessions sharing on-disk state) with 2,162 literature-consultation events; uses distributed grounding, adversarial review, and pre-/post-pilot stages with bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures; compared against pre-architecture baseline and no-pilot ablation.
AI.result: Autonomously produced three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism; identified structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism; characterized two paired failure modes.
AI.conclusion: The primitives, failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free guardrail that uses activation-space kNN classification from off-the-shelf LLMs to detect unsafe/off-topic prompts, achieving competitive F1 scores while running 2.7x-10x faster than fine-tuned alternatives, with rapid domain adaptation requiring only a small labeled bank (50 prompts) constructed in under 10 seconds.
AI.motivation: Existing guardrails rely on fine-tuning classifiers which suffer from low generalization and high inference latency; there is a need for a training-free, low-latency, and easily adaptable guardrail solution for LLM safety.
AI.method: kNNGuard extracts hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM and performs multi-layer kNN classification by fusing activation-space scores with embedding-space scores, using a small bank of 50 labeled prompts.
AI.result: Achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails across six domains; runs 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10x faster than fine-tuned safety classifiers; domain adaptation requires under 10 seconds.
AI.conclusion: kNNGuard offers a training-free, configurable, low-latency guardrail for LLM pipelines that is easily adaptable to new domains via a small labeled prompt bank, without gradient updates or fine-tuning.

title: ComplexMimic: Human-Scene Interaction Imitation in Complex 3D Environments
summary: Physics-based Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) imitation learning is crucial for embodied intelligence as it bridges the gap between kinematic 3D motions and real-world dynamics. However, most existing methods focus on simplified scene settings, leaving complex environments largely unexplored, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we focus on HSI mimicry in complex environments. Under this complex setting, we observe an inherent trade-off between successfully performing interaction and maintaining natural, physically plausible motions. To address this challenge, we propose ComplexMimic, a framework that reconstructs diverse HSI by interpreting imperfect MoCap data. First, we introduce a Dual Flow Strategy, which learns two complementary experts: an imitation expert for accurate motion tracking and an interaction expert for collision-aware adaptation in complex scenes. Second, naive multi-expert distillation, which treats all experts equally, often under-samples challenging behaviors, limiting effective learning. To mitigate this issue, we propose a difficulty-aware distillation strategy that adaptively weights supervision and prioritizes hard-yet-learnable trajectories guided by failure statistics and learning progress signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LuPan23/ComplexMimic.

AI.tldr: ComplexMimic is a framework for physics-based human-scene interaction imitation learning in complex environments. It uses a Dual Flow Strategy with two experts (imitation and interaction) and a difficulty-aware distillation strategy to balance motion tracking accuracy and physically plausible interaction, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing HSI imitation learning methods are limited to simplified scene settings and fail in complex environments, while performing interaction and maintaining natural motion presents an inherent trade-off that prior work does not address.
AI.method: ComplexMimic introduces (1) a Dual Flow Strategy with an imitation expert for accurate motion tracking and an interaction expert for collision-aware adaptation, and (2) a difficulty-aware distillation strategy that adaptively weights supervision based on failure statistics and learning progress to prioritize hard-yet-learnable trajectories.
AI.result: Outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets for HSI imitation in complex environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed difficulty-aware multi-expert distillation effectively resolves the trade-off between interaction success and motion naturalness, enabling more realistic HSI imitation in complex real-world scenarios.

title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
summary: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DRIFTLENS, a framework to measure how injected user-attribute memory (e.g., age, occupation) changes LLMs' reasoning trajectories on open-ended questions, finding medium-to-large reasoning drift across models that persists even when final answers appear fluent, and shows that GRPO/DPO post-training only partially mitigates this drift.
AI.motivation: Current personalization in LLMs focuses on final answer changes, but the impact of injected user-attribute memory on the underlying reasoning trajectory remains unexplored. The authors aim to quantify whether memory reshapes reasoning beyond mere content adaptation.
AI.method: DRIFTLENS: a ground-truth-free framework that maps each reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between no-memory trajectories and trajectories under injected user-attribute memory across 10 attribute categories (age, occupation, disability, etc.) and 4 LLMs. Validated against pragmatic noise, then applied to evaluate GRPO and DPO post-training methods for drift reduction.
AI.result: User-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor across all models and attributes, even when final answers remain fluent and plausible. Both GRPO and DPO reduce drift but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capabilities are model- and reward-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models, revealing a gap that existing alignment methods do not fully address.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

AI.tldr: An improved Fourier Neural Operator predicts time increments for 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection, achieving compact (314k params, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms) inference with higher accuracy than standard FNO baselines, though accuracy is limited by training data resolution.
AI.motivation: To improve the accuracy and efficiency of neural operators for modeling Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a key fluid dynamics benchmark.
AI.method: Modified FNO architecture that predicts time increments (residual learning) rather than full solution fields directly.
AI.result: 314k parameters, 1.26 MB model size, 7 ms inference time; higher accuracy than standard FNO; generalizes to finer meshes but accuracy limited by training data resolution.
AI.conclusion: Predicting time increments yields a compact, fast, and accurate FNO for convection modeling, with data resolution being the primary accuracy bottleneck.

title: Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics: Protecting Facial Privacy against Customized Diffusion Models
summary: The rise of customized diffusion models has fueled a boom in personalized visual content creation, but it also introduces serious risks of malicious misuse, thereby posing threats to personal privacy. Image aesthetics are strongly correlated with human perception of image quality. Motivated by this observation, we address facial privacy protection from a novel aesthetic perspective by degrading the generation quality of maliciously customized models, thus reducing facial identity leakage. Specifically, we propose a Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics (HAA) framework that exploits aesthetic cues at multiple perceptual levels. HAA consists of two key branches: (1) Global Anti-Aesthetics, which degrades overall aesthetics and generation quality by constructing a global anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and a corresponding loss; and (2) Local Anti-Aesthetics, which disrupts facial identity by using a local anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to guide adversarial perturbations toward facial regions. By integrating both branches, HAA achieves anti-aesthetic degradation from a global to a local level during customized generation. Extensive experiments show that HAA outperforms existing methods in identity removal, providing an effective tool for protecting facial privacy.

AI.tldr: HAA is a facial privacy protection framework that uses a Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics approach—with Global and Local branches—to degrade generation quality of customized diffusion models, thereby reducing facial identity leakage.
AI.motivation: Customized diffusion models enable personalized content creation but pose serious risks of malicious misuse and facial privacy threats. Existing methods lack an aesthetic-driven approach to degrade generation quality for privacy protection.
AI.method: The Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics (HAA) framework has two branches: (1) Global Anti-Aesthetics with a global anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to degrade overall aesthetics and generation quality; (2) Local Anti-Aesthetics that uses a local anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to disrupt facial identity by guiding adversarial perturbations toward facial regions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show HAA outperforms existing methods in identity removal, providing an effective tool for protecting facial privacy.
AI.conclusion: Image aesthetics strongly correlate with human perception of image quality, and degrading aesthetics at multiple perceptual levels is an effective strategy for facial privacy protection against customized diffusion models.

title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
summary:
Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement coordination semantics directly at the hardware level, based on the TB-CSPN framework, to achieve deterministic, bounded, and verifiable coordination in safety-critical real-time autonomous AI systems.
AI.motivation: Current agentic AI systems face fundamental limitations in software-mediated coordination (bounded latency, deterministic coordination, enforceable safety guarantees) when deployed in safety-critical real-time environments, necessitating a more predictable coordination approach.
AI.method: The authors map selected TB-CSPN (Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net) coordination mechanisms onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive in software while coordination semantics become deterministic in hardware.
AI.result: The architecture enforces temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware, without focusing on acceleration but on determinism and enforceability.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-enforced coordination (via FPGAs) offers a viable path to achieving bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous AI components in safety-critical deployments, separating adaptive semantic reasoning from deterministic coordination enforcement.

title: Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

AI.tldr: LLMs used as judges are biased (verbosity, position). The paper proposes Bayesian inference with bias covariates and a topk-aware active acquisition rule to identify top-k items under fixed comparison budgets, showing bias correction lifts recall for cheap/mid-tier judges from ~0.5-0.6 to 0.84-1.0, while frontier models show little bias.
AI.motivation: LLM judges used for pairwise comparisons are noisy and systematically biased (verbosity, formatting, position effects), so naive vote aggregation recovers a ranking of presentation rather than true quality. The goal is to identify top-k items under a fixed comparison budget.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) Bayesian inference over latent quality with judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position) regularized by a shrinkage prior; (2) Topk-aware active acquisition rule that selects comparisons to maximize uncertainty reduction about top-k membership, not full ranking.
AI.result: On a benchmark with 16 LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude), naive aggregation plateaus at wrong top-k on biased judges regardless of budget. Bias-aware model recovers true top-k; topk-aware acquisition achieves ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal rules. Bias correction lifts recall from ~0.5-0.6 to 0.84-1.0 for cheap/mid-tier judges; frontier judges show little bias.
AI.conclusion: Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap/mid-tier judges have strong verbosity bias that can be corrected; frontier judges show little bias so bias-aware modeling adds minimal value. The proposed active acquisition strategy is budget-efficient for top-k identification.

title: PWM-ArtGen: Part World Model for Articulated Object Generation
summary: The key challenge in articulated 3D object generation from a single image is accurately predicting the underlying kinematic structure. Existing methods either infer kinematic parameters directly from a static image that lacks dynamic part-level kinematic relationships, or estimate parameters from visual dynamics generated from a single image, which is prone to accumulated errors of two steps. Moreover, the limited scale and diversity of existing annotated datasets further hinder generalization to complex, real-world objects. To overcome these limitations, we propose to learn the joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters. Recognizing that articulated objects can be formulated as dynamic systems, we propose a unified Part World Model called PWM-ArtGen. To leverage unannotated data, this model couples action diffusion and image diffusion with independent diffusion timesteps, which enables visual branch co-training. We further curate a photorealistic dataset of 19.7k part-level image pairs without kinematic annotations, to support co-training. Experiments demonstrate that PWM-ArtGen substantially outperforms existing baselines in the resting state and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects.

AI.tldr: PWM-ArtGen is a unified Part World Model that learns joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters for articulated 3D object generation from a single image, using co-training of action and image diffusion with a new 19.7k photorealistic dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for articulated 3D object generation struggle with either inferring kinematic structure from static images (lacking dynamic relationships) or using two-step approaches prone to error accumulation, while annotated datasets are limited in scale and diversity, hindering generalization to complex real-world objects.
AI.method: Proposes a unified Part World Model (PWM-ArtGen) that learns joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters by coupling action diffusion and image diffusion with independent diffusion timesteps, enabling visual branch co-training on unannotated data. Also curates a 19.7k photorealistic dataset of part-level image pairs without kinematic annotations.
AI.result: PWM-ArtGen substantially outperforms existing baselines in resting state and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects.
AI.conclusion: The unified diffusion-based approach with co-training on unannotated data effectively addresses limitations in articulated 3D object generation, improving kinematic structure prediction and generalization.

title: Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. codes and data available at:https://github.com/nearpot/predictive-conformal-slip-monitoring
summary: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction, monitoring volatility of residuals from a per-driver Random Forest slip model, can serve as a pre-incident traction loss warning. The result is negative: zero precision and recall against 14 real incidents, with a 15.3% false-alarm rate. The exchangeability assumption is violated for all drivers.
AI.motivation: Conventional traction control only intervenes after the adhesion limit is breached. The authors investigate whether a statistically grounded early-warning signal (based on conformal prediction) could predict gross traction loss before it occurs.
AI.method: Rolling Split Conformal Prediction applied to residuals from per-driver Random Forest models of expected slip. Uses real FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions as ground-truth incident labels. Evaluates over 19 drivers, 55,563 telemetry samples. Compared against static 95th-percentile threshold baseline. Ljung-Box test used to check exchangeability.
AI.result: Mean precision = 0.0, mean recall = 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents. Flags 15.3% of all samples as anomalous. Static baseline performs no better. Ljung-Box p < 0.001 for all 19 drivers, violating the exchangeability assumption.
AI.conclusion: The conformal-volatility approach fails as an early-warning system due to high false-alarm rate and violated statistical assumptions. The authors report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding and outline requirements for a genuinely predictive version.

title: Embracing Intra-Class Heterogeneity for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation: From Diversity to Precision
summary: Due to the scarcity of expert-annotated data, Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation (SSMIS) has emerged as a promising approach. Many anatomical structures in medical images exhibit significant intra-class heterogeneity, with different regions showing heterogeneous intensity patterns within the same structure. However, existing methods inadequately exploit this intensity-manifested intra-class heterogeneity, resulting in uniform structural representations and imprecise segmentation. Furthermore, the scarcity of labeled data makes it more difficult to effectively capture such complex heterogeneity. To address this, we propose Multiple Prototype Contrastive Learning (MPCL), an SSMIS framework that possesses better diversity and better precision. It consists of three novel designs: First, we provide structural representations with better diversity and propose Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) that effectively models intra-class heterogeneity by generating multiple prototypes aligned with intensity characteristics. Second, we further enhance more diverse structural representations and build a solid foundation for more precise segmentation through Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) that systematically optimizes a more discriminative and generalizable prototypical space. Finally, we achieve segmentation results with better precision through Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) that efficiently promotes intra-class heterogeneity knowledge transfer from prototypical space to the segmentation network. Extensive experiments on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity demonstrate that MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods, especially under extremely limited labeled data.

AI.tldr: MPCL is a semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework using multiple prototype contrastive learning to address intra-class heterogeneity, achieving state-of-the-art performance on three datasets under limited labeled data.
AI.motivation: Existing SSMIS methods fail to exploit intensity-manifested intra-class heterogeneity in medical images, leading to uniform structural representations and imprecise segmentation, especially when labeled data is scarce.
AI.method: MPCL consists of three components: (1) Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) to model intra-class heterogeneity via multiple intensity-aligned prototypes, (2) Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) to construct a discriminative and generalizable prototypical space, and (3) Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) to transfer heterogeneity knowledge from the prototypical space to the segmentation network.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity show MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly under extremely limited labeled data.
AI.conclusion: Modeling intra-class heterogeneity via multiple prototypes and optimizing the prototypical space with knowledge alignment substantially improves SSMIS accuracy and robustness under data scarcity.

title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs (both reasoning and non-reasoning models), achieving faster computation and better ablation performance than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extracting multi-dimensional behavioral subspaces (e.g., refusal) in LLMs are computationally expensive, making them prohibitive for reasoning models that produce long reasoning traces.
AI.method: Adapt the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with a probe-informed initialization to identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces efficiently in seconds.
AI.result: RFM enables rapid subspace identification (seconds) on both reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models, and achieves better ablation performance compared to alternative methods.
AI.conclusion: RFM could serve as a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs, pending further validation of subspace relationships across methods.

title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

AI.tldr: ART-RL learns adaptive timestep schedules for score-based diffusion sampling by formulating it as a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem, improving sample quality over fixed schedules while generalizing across budgets, datasets, solvers, and pipelines.
AI.motivation: Uniform and hand-crafted timestep schedules for score-based diffusion sampling are fixed and suboptimal; there is a need for adaptive, learned timestep allocation to improve sampling efficiency and quality.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART) as a continuous-time control formulation that treats sampling clock speed as the control, with a Euler error surrogate objective. Introduces ART-RL, a randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time RL problem, with actor-critic updates derived from trajectory-based moment identities.
AI.result: ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong baseline schedules across low-dimensional and image generation tasks, while requiring only timestep grid changes. Learned schedules generalize across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive timestep allocation via ART-RL is an effective plug-and-play improvement for diffusion sampling, with theoretical equivalence guarantees and broad empirical generalization.

title: Comprehensive Robustness Analysis of LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection in Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent advancements in LiDAR-only 3D object detection have demonstrated improved detection accuracy over benchmark datasets. However, the adversarial robustness of these models remains untested. Very few adversarial robustness studies exist for LiDAR-only 3D object detection and unfortunately, even they are limited to legacy models. Moreover, there is a systemic gap in the existing evaluation frameworks that rely simply on mAP ignoring other structural and predictive factors. To fill this gap, we propose a holistic framework that evaluates adversarial robustness using two structural factors (point cloud density and point cloud localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego). Using this framework, we perform an empirical study and critical analysis on recent and legacy state-of-the-art models using adversarial attacks specifically designed for LiDAR-based models. Our key finding is that high-capacity, voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations than pillar-based detectors. Additionally, non-anchor-based detectors demonstrate poor adversarial robustness, which necessitates rethinking model training techniques. Overall, our results demonstrate that recent models are as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as their predecessors. Therefore, we argue that there is a need to improve the evaluation benchmarks for 3D object detection that not only reward architectural modifications for improving detection accuracy, but also evaluate whether the design choices improve adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a holistic framework evaluating adversarial robustness of LiDAR-only 3D detectors using structural and predictive factors, finding that recent models remain as vulnerable as legacy ones, with voxel-based detectors more susceptible than pillar-based ones.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial robustness studies for LiDAR-only 3D object detection are limited to legacy models, and current evaluation frameworks rely solely on mAP, ignoring structural and predictive factors.
AI.method: A holistic evaluation framework using two structural factors (point cloud density and localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego) to assess adversarial robustness of recent and legacy LiDAR-based 3D detectors.
AI.result: High-capacity voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations than pillar-based detectors; non-anchor-based detectors show poor adversarial robustness; recent models remain as vulnerable as legacy models.
AI.conclusion: Recent LiDAR-only 3D object detection models are as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as legacy models, highlighting the need for evaluation benchmarks that reward both architectural improvements for detection accuracy and adversarial robustness.

title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework that generates physically plausible indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments by using statistical priors of object distributions and a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes large objects, significantly reducing geometric violations compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based methods for 3D indoor synthesis fail to capture plausible object layouts in non-Manhattan environments because they struggle with non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity.
AI.method: (1) Statistical priors of object distributions guide training to improve environmental understanding; (2) A hierarchical layout strategy prioritizes large objects first, mirroring human design workflows and minimizing layout violations.
AI.result: SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods on both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments, validated on a new benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments.
AI.conclusion: SPG-Layout achieves balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility for complex non-Manhattan indoor scenes.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically probes 78 molecular substructures in chemical language models, finding that pre-training improves molecular structure awareness (especially in upper layers), randomly initialized models already encode ring structures, and fine-tuning on downstream tasks selectively enhances task-relevant substructures consistent with chemical theory.
AI.motivation: Chemical language models are widely used but it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode, motivating a systematic probing study to understand their internal representations.
AI.method: Systematic probing of 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized CLMs, analyzing representations across layers and after fine-tuning on two chemical downstream tasks.
AI.result: Pre-training improves molecular structure awareness, especially in upper layers; randomly initialized models already encode ring structures in the first layer; fine-tuning affects task-relevant substructures more than others.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training enhances CLMs' understanding of molecular substructures, and fine-tuning induces chemically meaningful changes in representations aligned with chemical theory.

title: HandsOnWorld: Unconstrained Egocentric Video Generation with Camera-Disentangled Hand Control
summary: We present HandsOnWorld, a framework for hand-controlled egocentric video generation that forgoes multi-view and marker-based motion capture, learning instead from unconstrained monocular video. Such generality is bottlenecked by the scarcity of scalable 3D hand annotations: large egocentric corpora lack finger-level labels, whereas precise hand datasets are confined to narrow, instrumented settings, limiting prior hand-controlled generators to restricted scene distributions. We instead annotate 3D hands directly on in-the-wild egocentric video through monocular reconstruction, introducing a protagonist-centered annotation pipeline that filters the reconstructions at the action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels to build EgoVid-Pro, a dataset of clean, protagonist-only hand trajectories spanning 103K clips and roughly 12M frames across diverse everyday scenes. To resolve the camera-hand entanglement induced by large ego-motion, we further propose the Plücker Hand Map, a 3D-aware control signal that extends Plücker-ray representations from camera rays to the hand surface, disentangling camera and hand motion at the representation level. Experiments show that \method surpasses prior hand-controlled generators in reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy, and generalizes to out-of-distribution everyday scenes beyond the laboratory datasets on which prior methods rely.

AI.tldr: HandsOnWorld is a framework for hand-controlled egocentric video generation that learns from unconstrained monocular video using a protagonist-centered annotation pipeline and Plücker Hand Map to disentangle camera and hand motion, achieving state-of-the-art results on diverse everyday scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing hand-controlled video generators are limited because they rely on scarce 3D hand annotations—large egocentric datasets lack finger-level labels, while precise hand datasets are confined to narrow, instrumented settings. The goal is to enable hand-controlled egocentric video generation from unconstrained monocular video without multi-view or marker-based motion capture.
AI.method: (1) A protagonist-centered annotation pipeline that annotates 3D hands directly on in-the-wild egocentric video via monocular reconstruction, filtering at action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels to build EgoVid-Pro (103K clips, ~12M frames). (2) Plücker Hand Map, a 3D-aware control signal extending Plücker-ray representations from camera rays to the hand surface to disentangle camera and hand motion.
AI.result: HandsOnWorld surpasses prior hand-controlled generators in reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy, and generalizes to out-of-distribution everyday scenes beyond the laboratory datasets on which prior methods rely.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully learns from unconstrained monocular egocentric video, overcoming the scarcity of 3D hand annotations and camera-hand entanglement, enabling robust generalization to diverse real-world scenes.

title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
summary: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) for grading Linux/bash command responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC=0.888). Agreement declined with taxonomy level; rubric quality mattered more than model choice.
AI.motivation: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains challenging due to rising enrollments making manual grading impractical and rule-based autograders failing to handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation.
AI.method: Four LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) were tested with two prompt variants (minimal baseline and rubric-enhanced) on 1200 real student responses from second-year Computer Engineering students, graded by three expert instructors. A four-level cognitive taxonomy (L1–L4) combining cognitive complexity and operational impact was adopted.
AI.result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888, MAE=0.10, Bland-Altman bias=-0.014). Agreement declined consistently at higher taxonomy levels. Rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice across all models.
AI.conclusion: Question complexity is a reliable predictor of LLM grading difficulty. The taxonomy-based framework determines which questions suit AI-assisted grading and which require human review, providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

title: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
summary: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

AI.tldr: A stacking ensemble machine learning model (Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM) and an artificial neural network are developed to detect early-stage Alzheimer's disease using ADNI data, with iterative imputation for missing values, Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance, and wrapper/embedded feature selection. The ANN achieved the best performance across precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC, identifying key biomarkers for early diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease is often diagnosed late because early symptoms mimic normal aging. Since no cure exists, early detection is critical for better disease management and timely intervention.
AI.method: ADNI dataset; iterative imputation for missing values; Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance; wrapper and embedded feature selection; stacking ensemble (Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM) and artificial neural network; evaluation via precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The artificial neural network outperformed the stacking ensemble model across all metrics (precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC) for early-stage Alzheimer's detection.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning, particularly artificial neural networks, can effectively detect early-stage Alzheimer's using multimodal clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging data, and help identify important biomarkers for early diagnosis.

title: DeepGaze3.5-VL: Modeling Scanpaths via Autoregressive Token Prediction
summary: Understanding human visual attention on a scene over time has applications in domains such as interface design and inferring cognitive states. Modeling visual scanpaths has historically relied on specialized architectures with hand-crafted priors. While these architectures can model fixation sequences, their rigid structural biases restrict easy extendability and flexible conditioning. For instance, integrating task-specific instructions or adapting to distinct viewer identities requires custom, disjoint architectural additions. We frame scanpath prediction purely as a discrete sequence modeling task. By mapping coordinates into a text vocabulary, we leverage the pretrained representations of Vision-Language Models. This framing absorbs diverse factors of variation: simple prompting allows for global conditioning, such as providing viewer identities to capture personalized biases, or task-specific objectives like visual search. The framework can also integrate per-fixation attributes, such as individual fixation durations, alongside spatial locations. The autoregressive alignment enables the scalable, exact computation of per-fixation log-likelihoods, directly equivalent to the commonly used Information Gain (IG) metric. Our model, DeepGaze3.5-VL, establishes a new state-of-the-art across multiple datasets, achieving 2.18 bits of IG on MIT1003, a 46% improvement over DeepGaze III. This advantage persists even when baselines use identical high-capacity vision encoders. Beyond predictive performance, our generative framework serves as a powerful computational tool for direct behavioral interventions, allowing for controlled in-silico simulations that would be experimentally difficult or impossible to conduct in vivo. We demonstrate this ability by performing controlled interventions on the durations of pre-saccadic fixations, recovering known oculomotor phenomena purely from data.

AI.tldr: DeepGaze3.5-VL reframes scanpath prediction as discrete sequence modeling using Vision-Language Models, achieving state-of-the-art 2.18 bits IG on MIT1003 (46% improvement over DeepGaze III) and enabling controlled behavioral interventions through simple prompting.
AI.motivation: Existing scanpath models rely on specialized architectures with hand-crafted priors that limit extendability and flexible conditioning, requiring custom additions for task-specific instructions or viewer identities.
AI.method: Maps fixation coordinates into a text vocabulary and leverages pretrained Vision-Language Model representations, treating scanpath prediction as an autoregressive discrete sequence modeling task with simple prompting for conditioning.
AI.result: Achieves 2.18 bits of Information Gain on MIT1003 (46% improvement over DeepGaze III), sets new SOTA across multiple datasets, and demonstrates controlled in-silico interventions recovering known oculomotor phenomena.
AI.conclusion: A generative framework for scanpath prediction that is more flexible, extendable, and achieves superior predictive performance while serving as a tool for behavioral interventions.

title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting where agents iteratively improve executable policies under a fixed interaction budget. The authors build EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark from compact RL environments, and show GPT-5.5 achieves top scores across all 16 environments. They also provide trajectory-level diagnostics revealing how agents allocate budget and convert feedback into policy refinements.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations collapse policy improvement into a final score or conflate it with open-ended software engineering, lacking a controlled setting to isolate how agents iteratively refine executable policies through feedback.
AI.method: The authors design Autonomous Policy Evolution where a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. They instantiate this in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark of compact interactive RL environments, and evaluate agents on policy improvement trajectories.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments in EvoPolicyGym.
AI.conclusion: Strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, as revealed by trajectory-level diagnostics.

title: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 28 pages, 5 figures
summary: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that uses dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. The method includes INR2JLS for downstream tasks, achieving ~10% improvement in INR classification accuracy on CIFAR-100-INR over state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for analyzing weight spaces of neural networks often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer inference processing. Efficiently handling high-dimensional weight spaces remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors propose representing neural network parameters as dynamic graphs to capture temporal dynamics of inference, processed by a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder). They also develop INR2JLS to map implicit neural representations into a joint latent space for downstream tasks.
AI.result: The approach achieves significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR dataset.
AI.conclusion: Preserving the sequential nature of neural processing through dynamic graph representations effectively improves performance on weight space analysis and INR classification tasks.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
summary:
In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

AI.tldr: G-RRM integrates symbol-equivariant recurrent reasoning models (SE-RRMs) with symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0) for constraint satisfaction. Neural guidance improves solver efficiency when problems have expansive search spaces and solvers can dynamically overwrite branching hints. Under these conditions, backtracking achieves 33.3× speedup and Glucose 4.1 achieves 1.70× speedup on 9×9 Sudoku, while CaDiCaL (which cannot overwrite hints) shows no significant speedup.
AI.motivation: To investigate when and how neural guidance from SE-RRMs (symbol-equivariant reasoning models) can improve the search efficiency of classical symbolic constraint satisfaction solvers.
AI.method: Proposes G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic approach that uses SE-RRMs as neural solvers to generate full solution proposals, which guide symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0). Analyzes conditions under which neural guidance improves efficiency: (1) expansive combinatorial search space, (2) solver architecture capable of dynamically overwriting branching choices.
AI.result: On 9×9 Sudoku (SE-RRM solves 91.1%): backtracking speeds up 33.3×, Glucose 4.1 speeds up 1.70× (median, p<0.001). Glucose 4.1 retains 1.17× speedup on perfect-hint 25×25 grids. CaDiCaL 3.0.0 shows no significant speedup (median 1.02×, n.s.) and slight mean slowdown (0.90×) on 9×9.
AI.conclusion: Neural guidance translates into practical speedups only when both conditions are met (expansive search space + solver can overwrite branching hints). Solvers that strictly respect injected hints (CaDiCaL) do not benefit from guidance.

title: Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

AI.tldr: DALorRA is a variational Bayesian sparse framework that applies stochastic masking to LoRA rank dimensions, shifting uncertainty quantification from dense parameter space to rank level, improving calibration of LLMs without sacrificing reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit overconfidence during task-specific fine-tuning, which hinders their trustworthy deployment. Existing uncertainty quantification methods operate in dense parameter space and are ineffective for fine-tuned LLMs.
AI.method: DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions of LoRA components, treating each rank-one component as a Bayesian unit. This enables Bayesian regularization during training (via variational inference) and ensemble-like calibration during inference (via Monte Carlo averaging of masked ranks).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy, outperforming prior calibration methods for fine-tuned LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Shifting uncertainty quantification from dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of LoRA is both effective and efficient for calibrating fine-tuned LLMs, enabling trustworthy deployment.

title: TCG-AR: Real-Time Multi-View Augmented Reality for Trading Card Game Streaming
summary: Trading card games are increasingly played and broadcast online, yet live streams remain mostly limited to flat top-down footage of the playing area. Augmenting such streams with virtual models of the played cards would improve the viewing experience, but most existing systems rely on instrumented playing surfaces and embedded chips, which are costly and impractical for casual players and large-scale events. In this work, we present TCG-AR, a novel real-time pipeline that augments trading card games using ordinary RGB cameras alone, without any physical markers or specialized hardware. Our pipeline detects, orients, and identifies the cards on the board, renders virtual content onto each card across all views, and can additionally compose a broadcaststyle view that summarizes the game state for spectators, streaming the augmented feeds to standard broadcasting software such as OBS. To train the detection, orientation, and identification models without manual labeling, we introduce an automatic procedure that generates annotated synthetic training data from a reference set of card images. Then, we evaluate several trained models on a new manually annotated dataset with real images, analyzing performance and runtime throughput that determine real-world usability. Overall, by relying only on commodity cameras and hardware, and by open-sourcing all code, models, and datasets, this work aims to serve as a reference for real-time trading card recognition and to make real-time augmented-reality streaming accessible to the broader community of players and streamers.

AI.tldr: TCG-AR is a real-time pipeline that augments trading card game live streams using only ordinary RGB cameras. It detects, orients, and identifies cards automatically, renders virtual content on them, and generates broadcast-style views. Synthetic data generation eliminates manual labeling, and all code/models/datasets are open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Existing augmented card game systems rely on expensive, impractical instrumented surfaces or embedded chips, making them unsuitable for casual players and large-scale events. The authors aim to make AR streaming accessible using only commodity cameras.
AI.method: The pipeline uses ordinary RGB cameras to detect, orient, and identify cards on the board via learned models. Synthetic training data is automatically generated from reference card images to avoid manual labeling. A broadcast-style view summarizing game state is composed and streamed to standard software like OBS.
AI.result: The authors evaluate multiple trained models on a new manually annotated real-image dataset, analyzing both performance accuracy and runtime throughput to assess real-world usability.
AI.conclusion: By relying solely on commodity hardware and open-sourcing everything, this work provides a reference for real-time trading card recognition and aims to democratize AR streaming for the broader player and streamer community.

title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
summary: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

AI.tldr: LLM agents show systematic divergence between public utterances and off-the-record (OTR) thoughts when placed in socially structured settings, with decision divergence rising from ~3% to ~40% under alignment-inducing conditions, detectable via stance, semantic similarity, NLI, and survey measures.
AI.motivation: To study whether social structure (role, audience, relational context) changes what an LLM agent expresses publicly vs. privately, even without explicit objective in the prompt, revealing emergent social conformity behavior.
